modules.doc:
std/arena: a typed memory pool (region). Values are appended to one growing array and named by
their `u32` index, and the whole pool is released at once with `reset()`, which keeps the
memory for the next round: a per-iteration tree costs no allocation after the first one.

Best with Copy structs that link to each other by index
(`struct Node { left: u32; right: u32 }`), the arena shape of Rust's bumpalo / typed-arena
programs. `u32` indices are half the size of pointers, so twice as many nodes fit in each cache
line. Indices stay valid until `reset()`.
modules.summary: std/arena: a typed memory pool (region).

modules.doc:
std/bigint: arbitrary-precision integers (JS `BigInt`), backed by the runtime (dashu-int).

Velt has no operator overloading, so arithmetic is methods: `a.add(b)` returns a new BigInt
like JS `a + b`; `a.addAssign(b)` changes `a` in place like `a += b`, reusing its buffer (hot
loops such as a pidigits spigot should use the in-place forms). The arithmetic operations
have machine-integer twins (`mulInt(10)`, `mulIntAssign(k)`) that skip building a BigInt for
the small operand. Division truncates and `rem` takes the dividend's sign, like JS; dividing
by zero panics with a RangeError, as JS throws one. A negative shift count panics with a
RangeError too, where JS shifts the other way (`1n << -1n` is `0n`).

A BigInt owns a runtime handle: `clone()` copies the number, `[Symbol.dispose]()` frees it.
modules.summary: std/bigint: arbitrary-precision integers (JS `BigInt`), backed by the runtime (dashu-int).

modules.doc:
std/channel: `Channel<T>`, a typed queue between tasks (docs/std/channel.md). Any number of
tasks may send and receive through clones of one channel. A bounded channel makes `send` wait
while it is full (backpressure); an unbounded one never waits. `close()` ends the stream:
sends fail from then on, and receivers get what is queued, then `null`.

A sent value crosses to the receiver's task like a `spawn` argument: it moves when the sender
no longer uses it, and is deep-copied otherwise (objects are never shared between tasks).

`Channel<T>` is a handle struct, like `TcpStream` (docs/std/README.md "Handles"): copies share
one channel, so pass it to producers and consumers (also `spawn`ed tasks) freely. Close it
when done: a closed channel is freed once it is drained, and an unclosed one lives until the
program ends. Values nobody receives are dropped when the program ends.
modules.summary: std/channel: `Channel<T>`, a typed queue between tasks (docs/std/channel.md).

std/child_process: run other programs (rt_abi_async.md §14.3).

`exec` / `execSync` run a program to completion and return its exit code and output;
`execShell` goes through the platform shell (`sh -c`, `cmd /C`). `spawn` starts a program
with configurable stdio and returns a `ChildProcess` whose pipes are read and written with
promises. Programs are found through `PATH`; arguments are passed as-is (no shell quoting).
A non-zero exit code is not an error (check `code`); failing to start the program throws
`IoError` (e.g. code "ENOENT", message "spawn <program>: …").
modules.summary: std/child_process: run other programs (rt_abi_async.md §14.3).

modules.doc:
std/cli: command-line argument parsing (Node's `util.parseArgs` rules, commander-style API).

Build a parser, then parse an argv array (usually `args()` from std/process):

  const p = new ArgParser("tool", "Does things")
    .flag("verbose", { short: "v", help: "Chatty output" })
    .option("out", { short: "o", default: "out.txt", help: "Output file" })
    .positional("input", "File to read");
  const a = p.parse(args());
  if (a.flag("help")) { console.log(p.help()); return; }

Builder methods change the parser and return it, so they chain (`p.flag(...)` alone also works).
Accepted syntax: `--name`, `--name=value`, `--name value`, `--no-name` (flag set to false),
`-v`, `-abc` (short flags clustered), `-o value` / `-ovalue` (short option, value attached or
next), `--` (everything after is positional) and `-` (a positional). An option's value is
taken verbatim even if it starts with `-`. Repeated options keep every value (`getAll`).
Every parser has `-h, --help`.
modules.summary: std/cli: command-line argument parsing (Node's `util.parseArgs` rules, commander-style API).

velt:collections/btree/check: the invariants of a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), for
tests. Walks the tree from the root with the range each node covers and reports the first
broken invariant: keys in order and inside their node's range, node fill, the leaf chain, each
node's prefix (at most the one its range gives, `Pool.prefixFor`), each word (two bytes of its
key past the prefix, `EMPTY` in unused slots), and the smallest and the largest key with their
windows (velt:collections/btree/edges), separators that are live keys, and unused slots that
hold the fillers.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/check: the invariants of a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), for tests.

exports.name: checkPool
exports.signature: function checkPool<K extends Comparable<K>, V>(p: Pool<K, V>): string
exports.doc: The first broken invariant of `p`, or `""`.
exports.summary: The first broken invariant of `p`, or `""`.

modules.doc:
velt:collections/btree/edges: the smallest and the largest key of a `Pool`
(velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

A node at the edge of the tree (the root, and the first and last node of each level) lacks a
separator on one side, so the separators alone would give it no prefix: for keys that all
share a long beginning (`user/…`, paths, URLs) its words would all be equal and every search
would compare whole keys there. The smallest and the largest key stand in for the separators
those nodes lack (`Pool.prefixFor`). That holds for keys between them, so every operation first
places its key against them (`edgeOrder`): a lookup of a key outside answers at once, and an
insert of one makes it the new smallest or largest first, giving the nodes along that edge
their prefix again (`noteEdges`). A delete of the smallest or the largest leaves the edge
prefixes as they are: a range that narrows keeps them true, if shorter than they could be.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/edges: the smallest and the largest key of a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

exports.doc:

1 above the largest, 0 between them (or when the map is empty, or keys have no words: no prefix
to keep true). The windows settle it unless they tie.
exports.summary: Where `t` (window `win`) lies against the smallest and the largest key: -1 below the smallest, 1 above the largest, 0 between them (or when the map is empty, or keys have no words: no prefix to keep true).

exports.summary: Before `key` goes in: makes it the smallest or the largest key when it is outside them (the first key both), and gives the nodes along that edge their prefixes for the wider range.

modules.doc:
velt:collections/btree/inline_key: `InlineKey`, the order-preserving bytes of a key that
`BTreeMap` keeps beside its keys, a few per key, to search nodes without reading the keys.

A key's encoding is a byte string that orders as the keys do: for keys `a < b`, `a`'s bytes
are at most `b`'s in byte order. Numbers encode big-endian (signed ones with the sign bit
flipped), `bool` as one byte, and strings as their CESU-8 bytes, the order of `<` on
strings. Shorter encodings read as zero past their end. Other comparable types get the
blanket implementation, which has no encoding (`hasInlineKey()` is false): the map compares
their keys in full. A type with an order of its own implements `InlineKey` with an `extend`
block (or `implements InlineKey`) to get the fast search.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/inline_key: `InlineKey`, the order-preserving bytes of a key that `BTreeMap` keeps beside its keys, a few per key, to search nodes without reading the keys.

exports.name: string
exports.doc:
Strings: their CESU-8 bytes (each UTF-16 code unit as UTF-8 would write it), whose byte order is
the order of the code units, `<` on strings. A string keeps its text as WTF-8, the same bytes
but for a character past U+FFFF (four bytes, from F0), which CESU-8 writes as its two
surrogates; so up to the first such byte the encoding is read where the string keeps it, two
ASCII characters to a word. Past one it is decoded (`cesuBytes`).
exports.summary: Strings: their CESU-8 bytes (each UTF-16 code unit as UTF-8 would write it), whose byte order is the order of the code units, `<` on strings.

modules.doc:
velt:collections/btree/insert: inserts into a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

An entry goes into the leaf its key belongs to; a full leaf moves entries to a sibling with
room (`shiftToSibling`), and only when both are full splits in two, the new leaf going right
of it under a separator, which may split the parent in turn, up to a new root. Moving entries
to a sibling instead of splitting keeps leaves fuller (B*-trees): about 85% instead of 70%
for random keys, so fewer leaves, less memory and fewer cache lines per entry.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/insert: inserts into a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

exports.name: insert
exports.signature: function insert<K extends Comparable<K>, V>(p: Pool<K, V>, key: K, value: V)
exports.doc: Stores `value` under `key` in `p`, replacing the value already there.
exports.summary: Stores `value` under `key` in `p`, replacing the value already there.

modules.doc:
velt:collections/btree/leaf: entries of a leaf of a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool),
internal.

A leaf keeps its keys and values in physical slots `0 .. n` in the order they came, its words
by physical slot too, and its rank order apart (`Pool.leafOrder`: rank → slot). An insert
appends at slot `n` and inserts the slot into the order; a delete moves the last slot into the
hole. So neither moves the other entries: an insert touches one key and one value line where
a sorted leaf would shift (and so read) every key and value after the new one. A search needs
no order: words below the target's give its rank, words equal to it give the slots of the
keys to compare. What works on ranks (walks, ranges, splits, merges) reads the order; entries
move between leaves by rank (`moveRanks`), so no leaf is ever sorted.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/leaf: entries of a leaf of a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

Finds the leaves of `keys[start .. start + m]` together: level by level, each key's next node
is prefetched once its slot is known, so it loads while the others search theirs. Then each
key's candidate slot in its leaf (`leafCandidate`, `NO_SLOT` for none), with its key and value

exports.summary: Finds the leaves of `keys[start ..

exports.name: moveRanks
exports.signature: function moveRanks<K extends Comparable<K>, V>(p: Pool<K, V>, from: u32, lo: usize, k: usize, to: u32, before: bool)
exports.doc:
Moves the entries of `from`'s ranks `lo .. lo + k` (its smallest when `lo` is 0, else its
largest) to `to`, all of whose keys are above them (`before`) or below them: into `to`'s free
slots from its count up, at its ranks `0 .. k` or after its own. The entries of `from` left in
slots past its new count move into the holes, so its slots stay `0 .. n - k`. Nothing else
moves: no leaf is put in rank order. Words follow their keys, at each leaf's present prefix;
a caller whose change of separators changes a prefix refreshes that leaf.
exports.summary: Moves the entries of `from`'s ranks `lo ..

modules.doc:
velt:collections/btree/line: `Line`, the 32 `u16` words of a B-tree node, internal.

A line is 64 bytes, four `u16x8` vectors: slots 0 to 30 hold a word per key (two bytes of the
key's encoding past the node's prefix, `EMPTY` past the last key) and slot 31 (`HEAD`) the
node's header, its count in the low 5 bits and its prefix (in bytes) above them. An array of lines
keeps each one in one cache line (an array buffer of elements that are whole lines is
line-aligned), so a node's search reads one line.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/line: `Line`, the 32 `u16` words of a B-tree node, internal.

modules.doc:
velt:collections/btree/pool: the nodes of `BTreeMap` (velt:collections/btree_map), internal.

A B+tree whose nodes live in flat pools, a struct of arrays, nodes linked by `u32` index:
node `n`'s keys are slots `n * F .. n * F + F`. Leaves hold up to `CAP` entries and link to
both neighbors; inner nodes hold up to `CAP` separators and `CAP + 1` children, every key of
child `i` at least separator `i - 1` and below separator `i`. The leaf pools are in chunks of
256 leaves, so they grow without copying (and hold at most a chunk unused). A freed node goes on
a free list. Leaf entries: velt:collections/btree/leaf; inserts: velt:collections/btree/insert;
deletes: velt:collections/btree/remove; the smallest and largest key:
velt:collections/btree/edges.

A node's 32 `u16` words (`leafLines` / `innerLines`, 64 bytes, each in one cache line) are
what a search reads first: slot `HEAD` holds the node's count and prefix, and the slots below
it, for keys with an order-preserving encoding (velt:collections/btree/inline_key: numbers,
`bool`, strings), two bytes of each key's encoding past the prefix all of the node's keys
share (`prefixFor`); strings keep the next two in a second line next to it, a four-byte
word in all. Vector compares count the words below the target's, which is its rank unless
words tie with it; only those keys are compared in full. So a level of a lookup reads one line
and one child index. Keys without an encoding are compared one by one.

Unused key slots hold `fill[0]`, so that the pools stay arrays of plain `K`; value slots
likewise (`vals`, with `valFill[0]`); unused word slots are `EMPTY`. A filler is the type's
blank value (velt:mem `Blank`: `""`, a number), which owns no memory, or for a type without
one a share of a live key or value. A deleted key or value is released: when a live
filler's entry is deleted or its value replaced, a live entry from the middle of the tree
gives new fillers (`refill`), a separator that is a deleted key that owns memory follows to
the next key, and the last delete drops the pools (velt:collections/btree/remove).
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/pool: the nodes of `BTreeMap` (velt:collections/btree_map), internal.

members.name: leafKeys
members.doc:
The leaves' keys, `F` slots a leaf, in chunks of 256 leaves (`LEAF_SHIFT`): slot `s` (`leaf * F +
i`) is `leafKeys[s >> SLOT_SHIFT][s & SLOT_MASK]`. A chunk grows only until it is full, so
the pools never copy their whole contents to grow, and hold at most one chunk unused.
members.summary: The leaves' keys, `F` slots a leaf, in chunks of 256 leaves (`LEAF_SHIFT`): slot `s` (`leaf * F + i`) is `leafKeys[s >> SLOT_SHIFT][s & SLOT_MASK]`.

members.name: vals
members.doc:
The leaves' value slots, addressed like their keys, an unused slot holding a share of
`valFill[0]`, the first value stored (as unused key slots hold one of `fill[0]`): a removed
value is dropped when its slot gets the filler. Values that own nothing take their own size
per slot, objects a pointer.
members.summary: The leaves' value slots, addressed like their keys, an unused slot holding a share of `valFill[0]`, the first value stored (as unused key slots hold one of `fill[0]`): a removed value is dropped when its slot gets the filler.

members.name: leafLines
members.doc:
Each leaf's words and header (velt:collections/btree/line), 64 bytes: leaf `l`'s line is
`leafLines[l >> LEAF_SHIFT][(l & LEAF_MASK) << lineShift]`. Keys with wide words
(`InlineKey.inlineWide`) keep the next two bytes of each key past the word in a second line
right after it (`lineShift` 1), so a search loads both as one 128-byte block (arrays of whole
lines are 128-byte aligned): one cache line on CPUs with 128-byte lines, an adjacent pair
elsewhere.
members.summary: Each leaf's words and header (velt:collections/btree/line), 64 bytes: leaf `l`'s line is `leafLines[l >> LEAF_SHIFT][(l & LEAF_MASK) << lineShift]`.

members.name: lineShift
members.doc: 1 when nodes keep two lines (wide words), else 0: set with the first key.
members.summary: 1 when nodes keep two lines (wide words), else 0: set with the first key.

members.name: leafOrder

Each leaf's rank order (velt:collections/btree/line `Order`), chunked as the lines are. A
leaf's keys and values sit in physical slots in the order they came; `leafOrder` gives the
slot of each rank (velt:collections/btree/leaf).
members.summary: Each leaf's rank order (velt:collections/btree/line `Order`), chunked as the lines are.

velt:collections/btree/remove: deletes from a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

A leaf below `MIN_LEAF` entries takes entries from a sibling that has more, or merges with it,
by rank (velt:collections/btree/leaf `moveRanks`, no leaf is sorted), and the parent loses a
separator, which may leave it short in turn (an inner node below `MIN_INNER` separators
borrows one or merges), up to the root; a root left with one child gives way to it. A leaf
whose range widens keeps its prefix when that still holds (`keepPrefix`, `mergeInto`), else
gets its words again; one whose range narrows keeps its prefix, true if shorter than it could
be. Inner nodes whose separators change get their prefix and words again (`refreshInner`); a
node that moves to another parent keeps its separators, so its words stay.
modules.summary: velt:collections/btree/remove: deletes from a `Pool` (velt:collections/btree/pool), internal.

std/collections/btree_map: `BTreeMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order
(`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

A B+tree of 32-slot nodes in flat pools (velt:collections/btree/pool): lookups, inserts and
deletes are O(log n) and touch a few cache lines per level; ordered walks follow the linked
leaves. Keys with an order-preserving encoding (`InlineKey`: numbers, `bool`, strings, and user
types that implement it) are searched by two bytes of it per key, eight keys per compare. Values are shared as `Map` shares them (objects are not copied); keys are shared too.

modules.doc:
std/collections/concurrent_map: `ConcurrentMap`, a map from `u64` or `string` keys to values
that many threads read and write at once, through a `shared` value: a B+ tree with optimistic
lock coupling (Leis et al., "The ART of Practical Synchronization"; bbtree's concurrent map
uses the same protocol). Built only on public std APIs: `Atomic<u64>`, velt:simd
(`loadOptimistic`), `Atomic.fence`, array `prefetch`.

Every node is 128 words of one `Atomic<u64>[]` arena (allocated whole by `create`), addressed
by index and never moved, so a reader that holds a stale index still reads a node and finds
its version changed. Readers write nothing. A delete that empties a leaf unlinks it, with any
inner nodes above it left with no other child, from the lowest ancestor that keeps a child,
and puts them on a free list (`spare`) that `alloc` takes from first. A node's version only
grows, through being freed and reused too, so a reader that read it before sees it changed.

Node layout (words):
  0: latch (bit 0 exclusive, then shared holders, the version from bit 21: velt:sync's
     `VersionLatch` word)
  1: meta: the number of keys | `LEAF_BIT` for a leaf | an inner node's level from bit 40
  leaf:  16-bit tags (hashes) of the keys, 4 to a word, at 2..16, tag 0 for an empty slot; key
         i at 16 + 2i, its value at 17 + 2i. Unsorted (a lookup only needs equality, a split
         sorts): a key sits in its home slot (other bits of its hash) when that was free, else
         in any free slot, so most lookups read the home pair without waiting for the tags.
  inner: an index at 2..8 (key 8g + 7 for group g), then from word 16 groups of 16 words, one
         cache line each: 8 keys, then the 8 children left of them (child 8g + j between keys
         8g + j - 1 and 8g + j); unused key slots hold `MAX_KEY`. A level reads the index line
         and one group line. Key i separates child i (keys below it) from child i + 1.
A reader reads a node's words with relaxed loads (several at a time with `loadOptimistic`),
then checks its version (`isUnchanged`), and starts over from the root when a writer changed
it. A writer takes the node's latch at the version it read, so a node that changed since
fails the take; a full node is split on the way down while its parent is held as well, so a
parent always has room for the separator.

String keys: the tree's key words are the strings' first 8 bytes in order (`inlineKey(0)`, so
a < b gives word(a) <= word(b)), and the strings themselves sit beside the nodes, in `skeys`:
a leaf's key in slot j at `node * SKEYS + j`, and the string of the separator left of a node
in its parent at `node * SKEYS + FENCE` (the node's fence: separator i of an inner node is the
fence of its child i + 1, so separators move between slots without their strings). Words that
tie are told apart by the strings: an inner node's separators with the key's word that are
greater than the key send it left of them (`backTies`, a binary search over the tied run), and
a leaf slot whose tag and word match is the key's only if its string is (`sameKey`). Tags and
home slots hash the whole string, so keys that share a prefix do not share tags. A reader reads
the strings as it reads the words, optimistically: borrowed, inside the epoch section the
compiler opens around the function that loads them, so one that a writer replaces meanwhile
stays readable until the section ends, and the node's version check after says whether what it
compared was the node's (a fence is read through the parent's child word, and changes only
while the parent is held: set before its node is linked, cleared when the node is unlinked or
becomes its parent's first child, whose fence is never read). A writer changes strings only
while it holds their node (or before the node is linked), and moves as few as it can: each one
replaced is retired to the epoch.
modules.summary: std/collections/concurrent_map: `ConcurrentMap`, a map from `u64` or `string` keys to values that many threads read and write at once, through a `shared` value: a B+ tree with optimistic lock coupling (Leis et al., "The ART of Practical Synchronization"; bbtree's concurrent map uses the same protocol).

exports.name: ConcurrentMap
exports.signature: class ConcurrentMap<K = u64, V extends Frozen = u64>
exports.doc:
A map from `K` keys (`u64` or `string`; `u64` when not written) to `V` values (`u64` when not
written) for many threads at once: share it (`shared(ConcurrentMap.create(n))`) and call its
methods from any task. A value other than a `u64` is boxed once, and read in place by `read`;
a string key is kept once, beside its leaf. Lookups write no shared memory, so readers on many
cores never slow each other; writers take a latch per node. A lookup waits (spins) while a
writer holds its node, so it is not lock-free. Its keys are kept in key ranges, but a leaf's
are unsorted and leaves are not linked: there is no ordered walk, iteration or size yet
(#1688). Its room is fixed when it is created, and given back as leaves empty.
exports.summary: A map from `K` keys (`u64` or `string`; `u64` when not written) to `V` values (`u64` when not written) for many threads at once: share it (`shared(ConcurrentMap.create(n))`) and call its methods from any task.

members.name: create
members.doc:
An empty map with room for at least `capacity` entries (its memory, about 40 bytes an
entry, and 17 more for string keys, is taken now; a string key's own copy when it is set).
A `set` that needs more room panics with a RangeError. A deleted
entry frees a slot in its leaf, and a leaf whose last entry is deleted is reused, so keys
that keep moving to new ranges (ids or timestamps that only grow, old ones deleted) fit for
as long as the entries present at once do. Leaves are not merged, though: entries spread
thinly over many leaves (most of a large map's keys deleted at random) can hold a node each
and need more room than their number. A `set` of a key the map holds can also need room,
when its leaf is full and splits first. Panics with a RangeError above 10^11 entries, and
for keys other than `u64` and `string`.
members.summary: An empty map with room for at least `capacity` entries (its memory, about 40 bytes an entry, and 17 more for string keys, is taken now; a string key's own copy when it is set).

modules.doc:
std/collections/deque: `Deque<T>`, a double-ended queue on a growable ring buffer: O(1)
amortized push and pop at both ends, O(1) indexing.

Slots are `(T | undefined)[]` (empty slots are `undefined`) with a power-of-two capacity plus
one spare slot at the end that is always empty. An element can't be moved out of an array
index, so taking one swaps it into the spare slot and `pop()`s it, then pushes a fresh
`undefined` back (no reallocation: the array's buffer keeps its capacity). Growing appends
empty slots and swaps the wrapped-around prefix up behind the old end, so elements are never
cloned or copied. A `T` holding `null` (`Deque<i64 | null>`) keeps its `null` apart from an
empty slot; a `T` holding `undefined` is a compile error (it could not be told from one).
modules.summary: std/collections/deque: `Deque<T>`, a double-ended queue on a growable ring buffer: O(1) amortized push and pop at both ends, O(1) indexing.

std/collections/priority_queue: `PriorityQueue<T>`, a binary heap ordered by a comparator.

`cmp(a, b) < 0` means `a` comes out first, so `(a, b) => a - b` is a min-heap and
`(a, b) => b - a` a max-heap (the `sort(cmp)` convention). Elements are only swapped inside the
heap array, never cloned; `pop` moves the top element out by swapping it to the end.
Elements that compare equal come out in unspecified order (a heap is not stable). The queue
keeps `cmp`, and a comparator may capture variables.
modules.summary: std/collections/priority_queue: `PriorityQueue<T>`, a binary heap ordered by a comparator.

std/collections/set: `Set<T>`, an insertion-ordered hash set with JS `Set` semantics, plus the
ES2025 set algebra (`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`,
`isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`).

Built on the prelude `Map<T, bool>` (Robin Hood index over dense insertion-ordered entries),
so elements compare as map keys do: numbers, bool and strings by value, objects (class
instances, object types, arrays, interface and function values) by identity, as in JS, and
tuples part by part. `add` takes ownership of the element; `values()` and the algebra results
hold the stored elements (objects shared, as in JS); `forEach` borrows.
modules.summary: std/collections/set: `Set<T>`, an insertion-ordered hash set with JS `Set` semantics, plus the ES2025 set algebra (`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`).

modules.doc:
std/collections/sorted_map: `SortedMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order
(`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

Two parallel sorted arrays searched by binary search: O(log n) lookups, O(n) inserts and
deletes (element swaps, cache friendly), which beats a tree for small and read-mostly maps.
Ordered queries (`first`, `last`, `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `range`) are O(log n) plus the
output. Keys are ordered by `compareTo`: as `<`, with a float NaN after every other value and
equal to itself. `set` takes ownership; `get` / `keys` / `values` / `entries` return clones
(unlike `Map`, which shares stored objects).
modules.summary: std/collections/sorted_map: `SortedMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order (`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

modules.doc:
std/compress/brotli/bits (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the input of a Brotli stream and
the bit reader over it.

The input is kept in one buffer of its own, followed by at least `PAD` zero bytes, so the
reader loads eight bytes at a time (one 16-byte vector load) without a check per byte; bits
past the input read as zeros. Whether a step read past the input is found afterwards, from the
bit position (`overran`): the decoder then waits for more input or reports a truncated stream.
The hot loop of commands.vlt copies `bits`, `count` and `pos` into locals and refills the same
way; the methods here are for the headers.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/bits (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the input of a Brotli stream and the bit reader over it.

exports.name: PAD
exports.doc:
Zero bytes kept after the input. A step of the command loop starts at most 8 bytes past the
input (at a byte position that a committed step reached) and reads at most 21 bytes more, so
its 16-byte loads end within 53 bytes of the input: twice that leaves a margin.
exports.summary: Zero bytes kept after the input.

exports.summary: The input buffer and the bit reader's position in it.

std/compress/brotli/command (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the insert-and-copy alphabet of
RFC 7932 section 5, one entry per symbol so that a command's lengths take one table lookup.

`COMMANDS[symbol]` is the insert length's extra bits (bits 0-7) and the copy length's (8-15),
then their base lengths (16-31 and 32-47). Symbols below 128 also reuse the last distance.
Generated from the RFC's tables of insert and copy length codes and its cells of 64 symbols.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/command (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the insert-and-copy alphabet of RFC 7932 section 5, one entry per symbol so that a command's lengths take one table lookup.

exports.name: COMMANDS
exports.doc: The lengths of each insert-and-copy symbol (see above).
exports.summary: The lengths of each insert-and-copy symbol (see above).

modules.doc:
std/compress/brotli/commands (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the commands of a compressed
meta-block (RFC 7932 section 9.3): literals inserted, then a back-reference copied or a word
of the static dictionary written.

This is where decoding spends its time, so the bit reader, the output position and the whole
command and block state live in locals for the length of the loop (one function, so that
they stay in registers), and prefix codes are decoded inline: one table lookup, two for codes
longer than 8 bits. Block switches, distances and dictionary words go through calls, with the
locals they touch written back around them.

The loop works in steps: a command's lengths, one literal (the last one of a command
together with the distance), a distance, a copy. After each it stops when the next byte to
load is past `safeEnd` or the output reached `limit`. The driver
(decoder.vlt) passes a `safeEnd` 16 bytes before the end of the input, so no step (at most 117
bits) reads past the input; near the end it passes -1, runs one step at a time and checks
afterwards whether the step needed more input than there is. A step's refill loads 8 bytes
at `pos`, which the zeros after the input (bits.vlt) keep inside the buffer.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/commands (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the commands of a compressed meta-block (RFC 7932 section 9.3): literals inserted, then a back-reference copied or a word of the static dictionary written.

exports.signature: function decodeCommands(s: State, safeEnd: i64, limit: usize): i64
exports.doc:
Decodes commands of the current meta-block from the cursor's stage until a step ends past
`safeEnd` (the input position) or at `limit` (the output position), the meta-block ends, or
the data is invalid. `s.out` has room for 64 bytes past `limit`.
exports.summary: Decodes commands of the current meta-block from the cursor's stage until a step ends past `safeEnd` (the input position) or at `limit` (the output position), the meta-block ends, or the data is invalid.

modules.doc:
std/compress/brotli/context (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the literal context lookup of
RFC 7932 section 7.1, for the four context modes in one table of 256 numbers.

Byte `m` (mode m: 0 LSB6, 1 MSB6, 2 UTF8, 3 signed) of `CONTEXT[b]` is what the previous byte
`b` adds to the context, byte `4 + m` what the byte before it adds. The two are disjoint bit
fields, so a literal's context is
`((CONTEXT[p1] | CONTEXT[p2] >> 32) >> 8 * mode) & 63`: two loads, one table for every mode.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/context (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the literal context lookup of RFC 7932 section 7.1, for the four context modes in one table of 256 numbers.

exports.name: CONTEXT
exports.doc: The context contributions of a byte, by mode (see above).
exports.summary: The context contributions of a byte, by mode (see above).

modules.doc:
std/compress/brotli/decoder (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the decoder's driver: it runs
the stream's parts in order (headers, uncompressed and metadata blocks, commands) as far as
the input and the room for output allow, and keeps the output buffer.

Input may stop anywhere. A step that can run out of it (a header, or a command step within 16
bytes of the input's end) starts from a saved state: when it turns out to have needed more
input than there is, the state is put back and the step is run again once more input came
(or, after the last input, the stream is truncated). Away from the end the command loop runs
without saving anything.

The output buffer keeps what back-references can still reach (the window) and what has not
been read; `brotliDecompress` keeps all of it, which is then the result.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/decoder (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the decoder's driver: it runs the stream's parts in order (headers, uncompressed and metadata blocks, commands) as far as the input and the room for output allow, and keeps the output buffer.

modules.doc:
std/compress/brotli/dictionary (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the static dictionary of RFC
7932 (appendix A) and its 121 word transforms (appendix B).

The dictionary is 122,784 bytes that are not all UTF-8, so it cannot be one string literal,
and an array literal of that many numbers is a source file of as many lines once formatted.
It is kept as two string constants instead, which the compiler joins into read-only data
(no module state, nothing built at run time): `LOW` holds each byte's low seven bits (ASCII,
escaped where needed) and `HIGH` its top bit, as `@` (bit 6 set) or a space. A word is put
back together sixteen bytes at a time: `low | (high & 0x40) << 1`. Both end with sixteen
bytes of padding, so a 16-byte load at any word's start stays inside them.

The strings were generated from the dictionary of the `brotli-decompressor` crate; the
transforms are packed as described at `TRANSFORMS`.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/dictionary (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the static dictionary of RFC 7932 (appendix A) and its 121 word transforms (appendix B).

exports.name: writeWord
exports.signature: function writeWord(out: u8[], at: usize, len: usize, wordId: usize): i64
exports.doc:
Writes the dictionary reference `wordId` (a distance past the window, less the window and one)
of copy length `len` at `out[at]`: the word with its transform applied. Returns the number of
bytes it stands for, or -1 when `len` has no words or the transform does not exist. Writes up
to 48 bytes past `at` (16-byte stores), which `out` must have room for.
exports.summary: Writes the dictionary reference `wordId` (a distance past the window, less the window and one) of copy length `len` at `out[at]`: the word with its transform applied.

std/compress/brotli/header (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the stream header and meta-block
headers of RFC 7932 (sections 9.1 and 9.2), and block switches (section 6).

A compressed meta-block's header sets up everything its commands are decoded with: the block
types of the three categories, the context modes and maps, and the prefix code tables, all
of them back to back in `State.tables`. It is read in one go, as one step of the decoder
(decoder.vlt starts it over when the input runs out before its end).
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/header (internal to velt:compress/brotli): the stream header and meta-block headers of RFC 7932 (sections 9.1 and 9.2), and block switches (section 6).

std/compress/brotli/prefix (internal to velt:compress/brotli): prefix codes (RFC 7932 section
3) read from the stream and turned into lookup tables.

A table is `u32` entries `symbol << 16 | length`, indexed by the next 8 input bits (the
root). A code longer than 8 bits has its root entry point at a second-level table instead:
`offset << 16 | (8 + bits)`, the offset relative to the root, indexed by the next `bits`
input bits. This is the reference decoder's layout; one table lookup decodes most symbols.
Bits arrive first-bit-lowest, so a code's table index is its bits reversed.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli/prefix (internal to velt:compress/brotli): prefix codes (RFC 7932 section 3) read from the stream and turned into lookup tables.

modules.doc:
std/compress/brotli: Brotli decompression (RFC 7932), the `br` content coding of HTTP.

`brotliDecompress` decodes a whole stream at once into one array that grows as the
meta-blocks' headers announce their lengths. `BrotliDecoder` takes the input in pieces and
hands out the output in chunks of at most the size asked for, keeping only the window that
back-references can reach and what has not been read, so a small input that expands
enormously never needs more memory than that. The decoder itself is in compress/brotli/.
modules.summary: std/compress/brotli: Brotli decompression (RFC 7932), the `br` content coding of HTTP.

three-bit header, stored blocks, and the fixed or dynamic Huffman tables of the others, whose

ends inside it, leaves the position as it was before the step (`SHORT`): a block header, a

modules.doc:
std/compress/inflate/checksum (std-internal): the checks a gzip member (CRC-32, RFC 1952 §8)
and a zlib stream (Adler-32, RFC 1950 §9) end with, computed as the output is made.

CRC-32 folds 64 bytes per step with carry-less multiplication where the CPU has it (Intel's
"Fast CRC Computation for Generic Polynomials Using PCLMULQDQ", the constants of
`crc32fast`), and otherwise takes eight bytes per step through the slicing-by-8 tables (one
16-byte load gives two steps); Adler-32 sums 5552 bytes between reductions, the most that
cannot overflow 32 bits.
modules.summary: std/compress/inflate/checksum (std-internal): the checks a gzip member (CRC-32, RFC 1952 §8) and a zlib stream (Adler-32, RFC 1950 §9) end with, computed as the output is made.

modules.doc:
std/compress/inflate/codes (std-internal): the inner loop of a DEFLATE block, the literals
and matches of its Huffman codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.5).

`fast` runs while 16 input bytes and a longest match (plus 16 bytes of slack) of output room
are left: it refills the bit buffer with one 8-byte load per symbol, without a branch (the
buffer then holds at least 56 bits, and a literal or length code with its extra bits and a
distance code with its extra bits take at most 48), and copies a match 16 bytes at a time when
its distance allows. `slow` decodes one symbol near the end of the input or the output, with
every bit counted: when the input runs out in the middle of a symbol it puts everything back
as it was before the symbol, to be decoded again once more input arrives.
modules.summary: std/compress/inflate/codes (std-internal): the inner loop of a DEFLATE block, the literals and matches of its Huffman codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.5).

modules.doc:
std/compress/inflate/huffman (std-internal): the decoding tables of a DEFLATE block's Huffman
codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.2), built as zlib's `inflate_table` builds them.

A table is indexed by the next bits of the input, least significant first, which are a code
read backwards: a root table of `root` bits holds every code that short (repeated for each
value of the bits after it), and a longer code's root entry points to a subtable indexed by
the bits after the root. An entry is one `u32`, so a symbol costs one load (two for a long
code):

- bits 0-3: the bits the entry's code takes at its level (the root's bits for a pointer);
- bits 4-7: the extra bits after a length or distance code, or a subtable's index bits;
- bits 8-12: what the entry is (`LITERAL`, `BASE`, `END`, `SUBTABLE`; 0 is no code);
- bits 16-31: the literal, the length or distance before its extra bits, or where the
  subtable starts.

A set of code lengths that does not make a prefix code is refused as zlib refuses it:
over-subscribed always, incomplete unless it is a single code of one bit (or no code at all,
for a block that uses no distances), whose missing entries stay 0 and fail if they are read.
modules.summary: std/compress/inflate/huffman (std-internal): the decoding tables of a DEFLATE block's Huffman codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.2), built as zlib's `inflate_table` builds them.

std/compress/inflate: DEFLATE decompression (docs/std/compress.md): raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951),
zlib (RFC 1950) and gzip (RFC 1952, several members in a row as one stream), in Velt.

`gunzip`, `inflate` and `inflateRaw` decode a whole stream into one buffer, sized from the
gzip trailer's length when there is one. `InflateDecoder` decodes a stream that arrives in
pieces into chunks of a bounded size, so a small input that expands enormously is still
handed out a chunk at a time. Both check the stream's CRC-32 or Adler-32.
modules.summary: std/compress/inflate: DEFLATE decompression (docs/std/compress.md): raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951), zlib (RFC 1950) and gzip (RFC 1952, several members in a row as one stream), in Velt.

zlib header (as browsers and Node's `fetch` accept both).

modules.doc:
std/crypto: SHA-256 and SHA-1 (FIPS 180-4), HMAC (RFC 2104), secure random bytes/integers
and constant-time comparison.

The hashes are Velt: where the CPU has SHA instructions (`velt:simd`, #1330: ARMv8 SHA2, x86
SHA-NI with SSSE3 and SSE4.1) whole blocks go through functions gated on them, which run the
bare instructions; elsewhere (other CPUs, WebAssembly, debug builds, `VELT_SIMD_DISABLE=sha`)
through portable rounds over `u32` words (integer arithmetic wraps, `>>>` is a logical shift).
Randomness comes from the OS generator through the runtime. SHA-1 is broken for collision
resistance: use it only for legacy protocols (WebSocket handshakes, HMAC-SHA1 in TOTP, git
object ids).
modules.summary: std/crypto: SHA-256 and SHA-1 (FIPS 180-4), HMAC (RFC 2104), secure random bytes/integers and constant-time comparison.

std/csv: RFC 4180 CSV parsing and writing.

The parser scans the text once with `charCodeAt` (the delimiter, quotes and line breaks are
ASCII, so an ASCII text is read inline); unquoted fields are slices of the input, quoted fields
are slices with `""` unescaped. Records end at LF, CRLF or a lone CR; a final line break does
not start another record, and a leading byte order mark (U+FEFF) is skipped. Quoted fields may
contain delimiters and line breaks. Fields are strings; no type inference.

std/datetime: `DateTime`, a UTC-first instant (JS `Date` without its local-time pitfalls), and
`Duration`.

struct, so it passes and stores like a number. Getters and `toISOString` are UTC; local time
(DST-aware, from the OS time zone) is opt-in: `localParts()`, `toLocalISOString()`,
`formatLocal()`. Months are 1-12 everywhere (unlike JS's 0-11). `parse` reads strings without
an offset as UTC (JS reads date-times without one as local time).

std/db: what database drivers share (docs/std/db.md): rows of any source into typed values.
A driver written in Velt
(a database's wire protocol parsed in place, a file format) implements `RowSource`, and
`readRows<T>` fills a `T` per row: each column the field of its name, as `JSON.parse<T>` fills
fields from keys, with the same conversions and the same messages for a row that does not
fit. The native drivers of std (velt:sqlite, velt:postgres) read their rows the same way.

For a row type of plain fields (numbers, bools, strings, `T | null` of those, `u8[]`) and a
source class whose methods do not throw, the compiler reads the rows column by column from
the source itself (`__intrinsic_read_rows`, null for any other type: nothing read): no text, no
copy beyond the values kept. Any other row type is read through the JSON text of the rows
(`rowsJson`), with the same result.

modules.doc:
std/encoding/binary_string: `btoa` and `atob` (globals, as in Node): Base64 of a "binary
string", whose code units are bytes (0..255).

Both read the string's UTF-8 bytes once: a code unit up to 0x7F is one byte, one from 0x80
to 0xFF the two bytes `C2`/`C3 xx`, and any larger one starts with a higher byte. `btoa`
collects the bytes in one buffer and encodes it with std/encoding's `base64Encode`; `atob`
decodes into one buffer of UTF-8 and turns it into a string with one runtime copy. Bad input
throws Node's `DOMException` (`InvalidCharacterError`, with Node's messages).
modules.summary: std/encoding/binary_string: `btoa` and `atob` (globals, as in Node): Base64 of a "binary string", whose code units are bytes (0..255).

framing undone (RFC 9112 §6): a `content-length`, chunks (`transfer-encoding: chunked`), or
everything until the server closes the connection.

`all` receives the rest of a body into one array: one sized from `content-length` (up to
4 MiB at first, doubled as the body arrives, so a length the server only claims costs
nothing), read into straight from the socket. A read straight into a piece of its own takes
at most 256 KiB, however much the body or a chunk claims to have left.
`next` hands the body over piece by piece, at most `max` bytes at a time. Once the body is
complete the connection goes back to the pool, unless the response said to close it.

uses it: the stream, a read buffer, and the request's signal, which every wait races so an
abort stops the request at once (the stream is then closed, never pooled). Between requests a
keep-alive connection is parked in the runtime's pool under its origin (`TcpStream.park`,
crates/velt_rt/src/net/park.rs), which every task takes connections from.

errors become `fetch failed: …` with the code of the error, as Node words them.

(zlib-wrapped or raw, decided by the first byte) and `br`, in any combination of up to five,
the last one undone first. A list naming another coding leaves the body as it is; an empty
body is empty in any coding; a body cut off before its compressed stream ends is an error.

A body read whole is decoded whole (velt:compress's one-shot functions, the output sized from
gzip's trailer); a body read piece by piece goes through a chain of streaming decoders, each
handing out at most `CHUNK` bytes at a time, so a small body that expands enormously still
arrives in bounded pieces.
modules.summary: std/fetch/client/decode (std-internal): undoing the codings a server compressed a body with (`content-encoding`), as Node's `fetch` does: `gzip` / `x-gzip` (several members), `deflate` (zlib-wrapped or raw, decided by the first byte) and `br`, in any combination of up to five, the last one undone first.

std/fetch/client/target (std-internal): a request's URL as the client uses it: its WHATWG
serialization (what `res.url` reports), where to connect, the `host` header and the
request-target.

WHATWG URL parsing costs more than the rest of making a request. Most URLs a program fetches
are already in the form the parser serializes them to (`http://host:port/path?query`, a
lowercase ASCII host), so `target` first checks for that form, in one pass over the text, and
takes such a URL as it is; anything else goes through `velt:url`. The check accepts only what
it can tell the parser leaves unchanged: a lowercase scheme, a host of lowercase letters,
digits, `-` and `.` (no IDNA label, and a dotted-decimal IPv4 address if its last label is a
number), a port only when it is not the default one and has no leading zero, and a path and
query of bytes the parser neither percent-encodes nor rewrites, without dot segments.
modules.summary: std/fetch/client/target (std-internal): a request's URL as the client uses it: its WHATWG serialization (what `res.url` reports), where to connect, the `host` header and the request-target.

std/fetch/client/wire (std-internal): HTTP/1.1 on the wire (RFC 9112): the request head the
client writes, and the response head it reads, parsed in place in the connection's buffer.

A request head goes into one byte array with its body when the body is small, so most
requests leave in one write. The headers `fetch` adds (`host`, `accept`, `user-agent`,
`accept-encoding`) are written unless the caller set them; the caller's names and values are
checked as hyper checks them (a token; no control characters but tab). The framing is always
the client's own, as undici's: `content-length` is written from the body (a caller's must
agree with it), and a caller's `transfer-encoding` is refused, so a header cannot make the
server read a different body than the one sent (request smuggling).

A response head is found by its blank line and kept as ranges of the buffer: the status, the
reason, and four numbers per header (name and value), so nothing is copied until a program
asks for a header. The headers the client acts on (`content-length`, `transfer-encoding`,
`connection`, `content-encoding`, `location`) are recognised as they go by.
modules.summary: std/fetch/client/wire (std-internal): HTTP/1.1 on the wire (RFC 9112): the request head the client writes, and the response head it reads, parsed in place in the connection's buffer.

modules.doc:
std/fetch/headers: the WHATWG `Headers` class of `fetch` (docs/std/fetch.md), also the type
of a server request's `headers` (std/http.vlt).

One flat list, `[name, value, name, value, …]`, in insertion order: names are lowercased when
they are added (header names are case-insensitive), values have surrounding whitespace
removed. The list is the runtime's format too, so a fetched response's headers arrive as one
array without being copied again. Lookups scan the list: a message has a handful of headers,
for which a scan beats hashing. A server request's headers stay in the runtime until
something needs all of them: `get` and `has` look one name up there. The headers of a
response made here start with the `content-type` its body implies held as a number
(`implied`), which a server hands to the runtime as it is; it becomes the list's first entry
when something reads or changes `content-type` or needs the whole list. The first header
added to an empty `Headers` is kept as it was given, outside the list (a new response
usually gets one or two: `res.headers.set("server", "velt")` makes no list and lowercases
nothing); a server hands it to the runtime that way, and anything else moves it into the
list first.

As in the standard, `get` joins repeated headers with ", " and iteration yields the names in
sorted order with repeats joined, except `set-cookie`, whose values are yielded one by one
(`getSetCookie()` returns them as an array). Unlike JavaScript, an invalid name or value is
not rejected here: `fetch` rejects it with `IoError` "EINVAL" when it sends the request (a
server answers 500). A fetched response's and a received request's headers are immutable, as
in JS: changing them stops the program (`TypeError: immutable`), a programming error like an
index out of bounds.
modules.summary: std/fetch/headers: the WHATWG `Headers` class of `fetch` (docs/std/fetch.md), also the type of a server request's `headers` (std/http.vlt).

modules.doc:
std/fetch/request: the WHATWG `Request` and `RequestInit` (docs/std/fetch.md): a request
`fetch` can send, made from a URL and the same options `fetch` takes, or one a server received
(std/http.vlt hands it to the handler).

A received request reads the runtime request (`VeltReq`, a registry key) lazily, as a
fetched `Response` does: its URL, method and headers are copied out the first time they are
read, and its body is received while it is read (`text()`, `json()`, `bytes()`, or chunk by
chunk through `req.body`). So a handler pays only for what it looks at, and the state only a
request made here has (body, redirect mode, signal, CA) is one null field. It is valid until
its handler settles (the server then releases the runtime request); what was read stays
readable.

modules.doc:
std/fetch/response: the WHATWG `Response` (docs/std/fetch.md): what `fetch` resolves to, what
a server handler returns (std/http.vlt), or a response built with `new Response(body, init)` /
`Response.json(data)`.

A fetched response holds the client's response (`Fetched`, std/fetch/client/fetched.vlt) whose
head has arrived; its body is received by the first `text()`, `json()`, `bytes()` or
`arrayBuffer()`, or chunk by chunk through `res.body` (a second read throws, as in JS). A
compressed body (`content-encoding: gzip`, `deflate`, `br`) arrives decoded. Dropping the
response closes the connection of a body nobody read. The status text and headers are made
into strings the first time they are read (most programs read neither), and stay readable
after the body was read. A built response
makes no `Headers` until they are read: the `content-type` its body implies waits in
`#implied`, and a server sends it from there.
modules.summary: std/fetch/response: the WHATWG `Response` (docs/std/fetch.md): what `fetch` resolves to, what a server handler returns (std/http.vlt), or a response built with `new Response(body, init)` / `Response.json(data)`.

std/fetch: the WHATWG `fetch` API (docs/std/fetch.md), global like in Node: `fetch`,
`Request`, `Response` and `Headers` need no import (std/prelude/global/fetch.vlt).

`fetch` resolves once the response's status and headers have arrived; the body is received
when it is read. The client is Velt code on velt:net (std/fetch/client/): HTTP/1.1 with
keep-alive connections pooled per origin, redirects followed as the Fetch standard says,
bodies decoded by velt:compress, and an `AbortSignal` that stops the request where it is
waiting and closes its connection.
modules.summary: std/fetch: the WHATWG `fetch` API (docs/std/fetch.md), global like in Node: `fetch`, `Request`, `Response` and `Headers` need no import (std/prelude/global/fetch.vlt).

modules.doc:
velt:fs/fd: Node's file-descriptor API (`openSync`, `readSync`, `writeSync`, ...), a module of
its own so that a program importing `velt:fs` does not compile it. It is Velt code over system functions (docs/reference/system-functions.md):
each call is one call of the C library, with nothing in between. On macOS and Linux; calling
it for another target is a compile error that names the system function it lacks.

Errors are Node's: an `IoError` whose `code` is the errno's name and whose message is libuv's
(`ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'a.txt'`), and `RangeError`s and `TypeError`s with
Node's messages for arguments it rejects.
modules.summary: velt:fs/fd: Node's file-descriptor API (`openSync`, `readSync`, `writeSync`, ...), a module of its own so that a program importing `velt:fs` does not compile it.

exports.doc:
The `IoError` for the errno `e` of the system call `syscall` (on `path`, if any), as Node
writes it: `ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'a.txt'`.
exports.summary: The `IoError` for the errno `e` of the system call `syscall` (on `path`, if any), as Node writes it: `ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'a.txt'`.

exports.signature: function openSync(path: string, flags: string | number = "r", mode: number = 0o666): number
exports.doc:
Opens `path` and returns its file descriptor (Node's `fs.openSync`). `flags` is one of Node's
strings (`"r"`, `"r+"`, `"w"`, `"wx"`, `"w+"`, `"a"`, `"ax"`, `"a+"`, ... and the `s`
forms) or the system's `O_*` bits as a number; `mode` is the permission of a file it
creates (before the umask).
exports.summary: Opens `path` and returns its file descriptor (Node's `fs.openSync`).

exports.name: unlinkSync
exports.doc: Removes the file `path` (Node's `fs.unlinkSync`; not a directory: `EPERM` or `EISDIR`).
exports.summary: Removes the file `path` (Node's `fs.unlinkSync`; not a directory: `EPERM` or `EISDIR`).

exports.name: closeSync
exports.doc: Closes the file descriptor `fd` (Node's `fs.closeSync`).
exports.summary: Closes the file descriptor `fd` (Node's `fs.closeSync`).

exports.name: readSync
exports.signature: function readSync(fd: number, buffer: u8[] | ArrayBufferView, offset: number | null = 0, length?: number | null, position?: number | null): number
exports.doc:
Reads up to `length` bytes into `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.readSync`): at
`position` in the file, or at the file's own position (which then advances) when `position`
is left out, `null` or -1. Returns the number of bytes read, 0 at the end of the file.
`offset` defaults to 0 and `length` to the rest of the buffer; a number is coerced as Node
does (`length` truncated to a 32-bit integer, `position` validated strictly). `buffer` is a
`u8[]` (Node's `Buffer`), a typed array or a `DataView`; `offset` and `length` count bytes of
it. Velt's typed API takes positional arguments, not Node's `(fd, buffer, options)` object.
exports.summary: Reads up to `length` bytes into `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.readSync`): at `position` in the file, or at the file's own position (which then advances) when `position` is left out, `null` or -1.

exports.name: writeSync
exports.signature: function writeSync(fd: number, buffer: u8[] | ArrayBufferView | string, offset: number | null = null, length?: number | null, position?: number | null): number
exports.doc:
Writes `length` bytes of `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.writeSync`): at
`position` in the file, or at the file's own position when `position` is left out, `null` or
not a valid byte offset (at its end for a file opened to append). Returns the number of bytes
written. `offset` defaults to 0 and `length` to the rest of the buffer. `buffer` is a `u8[]`
(Node's `Buffer`), a typed array or a `DataView`; a string is written as UTF-8, and its third
argument is then the position.
exports.summary: Writes `length` bytes of `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.writeSync`): at `position` in the file, or at the file's own position when `position` is left out, `null` or not a valid byte offset (at its end for a file opened to append).

modules.doc:
std/fs: file system access over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §5).

Every operation has an async form (runs on the runtime's blocking pool) and a `*Sync` form
(blocks the calling thread). Failures throw `IoError` (from "velt:io") with a Node-style `code`.
Paths and data are borrowed by the runtime and copied at the call, so the wrappers never copy.

Extern conventions (the lowering ABI of `declare function`, rt_abi_async.md §3.1): `string`/
struct params are passed as `const T*`; a struct result becomes a trailing out-pointer and the
runtime function returns nothing.
modules.summary: std/fs: file system access over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §5).

modules.doc:
std/fs_stream: reading and writing files in chunks (rt_abi_async.md §14.7), for files too
large to hold in memory or produced incrementally (logs, exports, line-by-line processing).

`openRead` gives a `FileReader` (bytes, text chunks or lines); `openWrite` a buffered
`FileWriter`. Operations run on the runtime's blocking pool like the rest of std/fs and
throw `IoError`. Like std/net's `TcpStream`, both are Copy handles (so `await r.readLine()`
can be called repeatedly; async methods take `this` by copy) released by `close()`: an
unclosed handle leaks until exit; after `close()` through any copy, the others throw
`IoError` `EBADF` and closing again does nothing. A writer's `close()` also flushes and
reports write errors.
modules.summary: std/fs_stream: reading and writing files in chunks (rt_abi_async.md §14.7), for files too large to hold in memory or produced incrementally (logs, exports, line-by-line processing).

std/hash: a stable, non-cryptographic hash (docs/std/hash.md) for sharding, bucketing and
consistent hashing. 64-bit FNV-1a: the same input gives the same hash on every platform, run
and version. It is not seeded, so it does not resist hash flooding (an attacker can choose
keys that collide); use `velt:crypto` where an adversary picks the input.

modules.doc:
std/http/server/parse: HTTP/1.1 request heads parsed in place (internal to std/http/server).

A connection reads into one buffer of its own (`Parser`); a request's head is ranges of that
buffer (`Head`), valid until the connection reads the next one, so nothing is copied or
allocated per request unless the handler asks for a string. The body is not waited for: the
request's reader (http/server/request.vlt) reads it as the handler asks. The end of a head is
found 16 bytes at a time (`velt:simd`: lanes equal to LF), and the headers the server acts on
are recognised by their length and one vector compare, letters folded to lowercase. Every
header's ranges are kept (four numbers each) for `header(name)`.

The byte strings the parser compares with are made per connection: module-level constants
that are not literals are module state, behind one process-wide lock (#1487).
modules.summary: std/http/server/parse: HTTP/1.1 request heads parsed in place (internal to std/http/server).

modules.doc:
std/http/server/request: `HttpRequest`, a request's head (parsed in place, http/server/parse.vlt)
and its body, read as the handler asks (internal to std/http/server, which exports the class).

The handler runs once the head has arrived; the body comes through `read()` (the next piece,
for uploads and proxies: nothing is held but the connection's buffer) or `body()` (all of it,
up to the server's `maxBodySize`). A body framed by Content-Length is read as it arrives; a
chunked one (RFC 9112 §7.1) is decoded, its extensions and trailers skipped. A client that
sent `Expect: 100-continue` gets `100 Continue` when the handler first reads. What the handler
leaves unread is skipped before the connection's next request (`finish`).
modules.summary: std/http/server/request: `HttpRequest`, a request's head (parsed in place, http/server/parse.vlt) and its body, read as the handler asks (internal to std/http/server, which exports the class).

modules.doc:
std/http/server/response: `HttpResponse`, `HttpStream` and `EventStream` (internal to
std/http/server, which exports them).

A response written at once (`send` and the like) goes into one buffer per connection, so the
responses to the requests one read brought leave in one write; the fixed parts of a head are
encoded per response and the `Date` value once a second. A streamed response (`stream`, `sse`)
writes its head at once and each piece as one chunk (`Transfer-Encoding: chunked`; to an
HTTP/1.0 client, the body ends with the connection). Its pieces are queued on the connection
(`writeBytesLater`): what the handler writes before it next waits leaves in one write, and
`write` waits while more than `QUEUED` bytes are still to be sent, so a fast producer waits for
a slow client (backpressure); a client that went away makes it throw and aborts the request's
signal (cancellation).
modules.summary: std/http/server/response: `HttpResponse`, `HttpStream` and `EventStream` (internal to std/http/server, which exports them).

exports.name: HttpResponse
exports.doc:
A response being written: `status`, `header`, then one of the `send` methods (the whole
response) or `stream` / `sse` (a body written piece by piece). One per connection, reused for
its requests; valid while the handler runs.
exports.summary: A response being written: `status`, `header`, then one of the `send` methods (the whole response) or `stream` / `sse` (a body written piece by piece).

so `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` are its own: a handler's are not sent, except a
Content-Length for the response to a HEAD request (the length a GET would get).
members.summary: Adds header `name: value` (a `content-type` replaces the default one).

members.name: stream
members.doc:
Starts a streamed response (default type `text/plain; charset=utf-8`): its head goes out
now, the body piece by piece through the returned stream (`write`, `end`). For large or

the piece being written.
members.summary: Starts a streamed response (default type `text/plain; charset=utf-8`): its head goes out now, the body piece by piece through the returned stream (`write`, `end`).

members.name: sendStream
members.signature: async sendStream(body: BodyStream, type: string = "text/html; charset=utf-8")
members.doc:
Streams `body` as the response (default type `text/html; charset=utf-8`): each chunk is
written as it comes, once the client took the one before. For `renderToStream` of
[velt:jsx](jsx.md): the markup above a pending async component reaches the client while it
loads. A client that goes away ends it quietly (the source is closed, so rendering stops;
`signal()` is aborted).
members.summary: Streams `body` as the response (default type `text/html; charset=utf-8`): each chunk is written as it comes, once the client took the one before.

members.name: sse

modules.doc:
std/http/server: an HTTP/1.1 server written in Velt on std/net (docs/std/http_server.md).

One task per connection. The connection reads into a buffer of its own; each request is parsed
in place there (http/server/parse.vlt) and handed to the handler with a response writer whose
bytes go into one buffer per connection: every response to the requests one read brought
(pipelining) leaves in one write. The fixed parts of a response head are encoded once per
connection and the `Date` value once per second; text goes into the buffer without a copy in
between. Nothing on the request path is module state (#1487).
modules.summary: std/http/server: an HTTP/1.1 server written in Velt on std/net (docs/std/http_server.md).

modules.doc:
std/http/stream: streamed response bodies, for a handler's `Response` whose body is a
`BodyStream` (rt_abi_async.md §14.17). Internal to std/http.

`pump` turns a runtime response's body into a stream and starts copying the `BodyStream`
into it as a promise of the handler's task (a stored promise starts at once and is not
cancelled when dropped, docs/language.md §8), so it keeps running after the handler returned
the response: hyper sends the status and headers, then every chunk as the stream yields it.
`flush` waits while the client is behind (backpressure); once the client has gone away, the
copy stops and leaves the `for await`, which closes the stream's source (an async generator's
`finally` blocks run).
modules.summary: std/http/stream: streamed response bodies, for a handler's `Response` whose body is a `BodyStream` (rt_abi_async.md §14.17).

exports.name: pump
exports.doc: Makes runtime response `r`'s body a stream and starts copying `body` into it.
exports.summary: Makes runtime response `r`'s body a stream and starts copying `body` into it.

modules.doc:
std/http: the HTTP server over the runtime (hyper; rt_abi_async.md §7). Handlers take the
global `Request` and return the global `Response` (std/fetch), as in Deno and Bun; the client
is the global `fetch`.

Server: `serve` hands the runtime a `VeltHandler` (init/poll/drop/state size/align/env). That
descriptor is produced by the compiler intrinsic `__intrinsic_http_handler(f)` from an async
closure literal `f: (raw: u64) => Promise<u64>` (`VeltReq` handle in, response out):
the closure's own state machine is the per-request state (result at offset 0), `init` writes its
initial state from `(env, req)`, `poll`/`drop` are the closure's `$poll`/`$drop`, and `env` is
the closure's heap environment (shared with in-flight requests; the runtime drops it once the
server is closed and its last request finished, so captured values' `[Symbol.dispose]()`
hooks run). `serve` wraps the user handler in such a closure, which hands it the raw request as
a `Request` that reads it lazily (std/fetch/request.vlt), releases the raw request once the
handler settled, and hands the returned `Response` to the request in one call (a complete
body), or builds it into a runtime response that a `BodyStream` body is then copied into
(std/http/stream.vlt), so the intrinsic only ever sees one closure type.

Handles (`VeltServer`: a `u64`, rt_abi_async.md §3.2) are released by the owning value's
`[Symbol.dispose]()` drop hook, which zeroes the handle so it runs at most once. A `Server`
stops only on `close()`; dropping it releases the handle but keeps it serving (like Node).
modules.summary: std/http: the HTTP server over the runtime (hyper; rt_abi_async.md §7).

exports.name: serve
exports.signature: async function serve<E>(opts: ServeOptions, handler: (req: Request, info: ServeInfo) => Response | Promise<Response, E> throws E): Promise<Server>
exports.doc:
Binds `host:port` (default host 127.0.0.1; port 0 = any free port) and serves `handler` in the
background. The handler returns a `Response`, or a promise of one (an `async` handler), as in
Deno and Bun. Handlers run concurrently, so like spawned tasks they must not mutate captured
variables (use `shared`). A handler that throws (rejects with `E`) gets a 500 response, and
the error is printed to stderr (like Deno's and Bun's `serve`).
exports.summary: Binds `host:port` (default host 127.0.0.1; port 0 = any free port) and serves `handler` in the background.

exports.summary: Whether `req` asks to switch its connection to `protocol` (an HTTP/1.1 `Upgrade` request).

exports.name: ConnectionUpgrade
exports.doc: What `upgradeConnection` returns: the connection, and the response to return from the handler.
exports.summary: What `upgradeConnection` returns: the connection, and the response to return from the handler.

exports.name: upgradeConnection
exports.signature: function upgradeConnection(req: Request, protocol: string, headers: HeadersInit | null = null): ConnectionUpgrade
exports.doc:
Takes over the connection of an upgrade request: return `response` (`101 Switching
Protocols` with `upgrade: protocol`, `connection: Upgrade` and `headers`) from the handler,
and from then on the connection is `stream`, a byte stream like any `velt:net` connection
(over TLS if the server is). The stream works once the response has been sent: its first
read or write waits for that (so what is written before goes out right after the response).
The client must wait for the response before it sends anything in the new protocol. Throws `IoError` "EINVAL" if `req` is not an upgrade request (`isUpgradeRequest`) or
its connection was taken already. Only HTTP/1.1 connections can be upgraded.
exports.summary: Takes over the connection of an upgrade request: return `response` (`101 Switching Protocols` with `upgrade: protocol`, `connection: Upgrade` and `headers`) from the handler, and from then on the connection is `stream`, a byte stream like any `velt:net` connection (over TLS if the server is).

modules.doc:
std/io: the error type and result plumbing shared by std/fs, std/net, std/http and std/process.

Runtime I/O functions (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §3) report failures as an `IoResult<T>`
with the C layout `{ i32 code; u32 pad; VeltStr message; T value /* @32 */ }`, which is exactly
the natural layout of the Velt struct below. `code == 0` means success: `message` is an empty
static string and `value` is initialized. Otherwise `value` is all-zero bytes, which every type's
drop glue treats as "owns nothing", so dropping a failed result is safe. Operations without a
value return `IoStatus` (the 32-byte `VeltErr` prefix).

Everything except `IoError` is std-internal plumbing; it is exported only so the other std
modules can share it.
modules.summary: std/io: the error type and result plumbing shared by std/fs, std/net, std/http and std/process.

exports.name: IoError
exports.doc:
A failed I/O operation (`Error` is the prelude base class). `code` is the Node-style name:
"ENOENT", "EACCES", "EEXIST", "EINVAL", "EILSEQ", "ETIMEDOUT", "ECONNREFUSED", "ECONNRESET",
"EADDRINUSE", "EPIPE", "EOF", "ENOTSUP", "ENOTDIR", "ENOTEMPTY", "EISDIR", "EBADF" (a closed
socket, file stream, child process or WebSocket handle) or "UNKNOWN".
exports.summary: A failed I/O operation (`Error` is the prelude base class).

modules.doc:
velt:json/reader — the pull reader under the decoders `JSON.parse<T>` compiles for each type.

The reader lexes its source on demand. The first failure is sticky: every later call fails
too, and `message` turns it into the `JsonError` message. Commas and colons are handled by
`nextKey` / `arrayNext`: the reader only needs to know whether the last token it consumed
was an opening bracket.

A driver's rows (std/db) are read by the runtime's row reader: such a reader starts out
failed (`ROWS`), so every method takes its failure branch, which forwards to the row reader;
reading text pays nothing for it.

Port of crates/velt_rt/src/json/reader.rs and error.rs (#1668), with the same results and
messages.
modules.summary: velt:json/reader — the pull reader under the decoders `JSON.parse<T>` compiles for each type.

velt:json/scan — byte-level JSON lexing (RFC 8259) for the pull reader, skipping and

asks for the text); only strings with escapes are decoded. Escapes decode to UTF-16 code

offsets.

exports.name: blankComments
exports.doc:

into spaces (newlines kept), so every byte keeps its offset and the scanner never meets a
comment: strict JSON pays nothing for JSONC. An unclosed `/*` and a `/` that starts no comment
stay, so the scan fails at that byte, as it did when the scanner skipped comments itself.

modules.doc:
velt:json/tape — a parsed JSON document as one flat tape (#1660, part of #1655): what a
`JsonValue` from `JSON.parseValue` reads. No allocation per value: two words per value in one
array, numbers decoded once, strings left in the source until a reader asks for one (only
strings with escapes are decoded while parsing), and each array's elements and each object's
keys listed together in one array of positions, so `at(i)` is O(1).

A tape's values never change after it is built (only `find` adds the hash index of a large
object it searches); values share it. Editing a value (`set`, `push`, …) turns that value into
the runtime's tree (prelude `JsonValue`), so it never shows through the tape.
modules.summary: velt:json/tape — a parsed JSON document as one flat tape (#1660, part of #1655): what a `JsonValue` from `JSON.parseValue` reads.

exports.name: T_NULL
exports.doc: Value kinds (the low byte of a value's first word).
exports.summary: Value kinds (the low byte of a value's first word).

exports.name: Tape
exports.doc:
A parsed document. Value `v`'s words are `words[2v]` (kind, and a container's member count
from bit 32) and `words[2v + 1]` (a number's bits, a string's range or decoded index, a
container's first position in `kids`). An array's `kids` are its elements; an object's are its
key strings, each followed on the tape by its value (`key + 1`). Value 0 is the root.

Every lookup is O(1) but `find` in a small object (at most `INDEX_THRESHOLD` keys, compared in
place), so walking any value is linear in its size.

Appends value `v` as compact JSON text (`JSON.stringify`) to the builder `out`. Every call
that takes `out` gets no argument that is itself a call (it would make a copy of `out`

the parser allowed writes without running out of native stack. The text is gathered in a
byte array handed to the builder in chunks: punctuation, strings and numbers cost stores,
not a call each.

arrays and objects (0: no limit); `jsonc` has the reader's `FLAG_COMMENTS` (16) and

modules.doc:
velt:json/writer — what `JSON.stringify<T>` writes for numbers and strings, in Velt (#1668).

The writers append to the string builder of the glue the compiler generates (`out`, a
`VeltStrBuf` the functions only pass on to the builder's primitives, never read: every call
passes it first, with no argument after it that is a call) and write
exactly what `JSON.stringify` writes: numbers as JavaScript prints them (`null` for NaN and
the infinities), strings quoted, with `"`, `\`, control characters and lone surrogates
escaped (well-formed `JSON.stringify`).

Port of velt_text's json_escape.rs and the JSON number path of fmt.rs.
modules.summary: velt:json/writer — what `JSON.stringify<T>` writes for numbers and strings, in Velt (#1668).
