exports.doc: A double as `m / 10^k` with a sign, when JSON writes it from those digits (`ok`).
exports.summary: A double as `m / 10^k` with a sign, when JSON writes it from those digits (`ok`).

exports.name: shortNumber
exports.doc:
`x` (finite) as the digits `JSON.stringify` writes for it without an exponent, when it has at
most 15 significant digits, between 10^-6 and 10^15; else `ok` false (the general printer).
At most 15 significant digits name a single double (decimals that close are farther apart
than doubles), so if `a = |x|` is such a decimal, it is the integer `m` nearest `a * 10^top`,
at the largest scale `top` that keeps that product below 10^15, over 10^top: the product is
within 0.18 of `m` (`a`'s own rounding, below 2^-53 of it, is at most 0.111 there, the
product's half an ulp at most 0.0625), and dividing back is correctly rounded, so it gives `a`
exactly when `m`'s digits name `a`. Those digits without trailing zeros are JavaScript's
shortest; at 10^-6 and above JavaScript writes them without an exponent. One multiply and one
divide, whatever the digits.
exports.summary: `x` (finite) as the digits `JSON.stringify` writes for it without an exponent, when it has at most 15 significant digits, between 10^-6 and 10^15; else `ok` false (the general printer).

exports.name: putDecimal
exports.signature: function putDecimal(buf: u8[], o: usize, neg: bool, m: u64, k: usize): usize
exports.doc:
Writes `m / 10^k` (`m` below 10^15) with a `-` when `neg` and `m` is not 0 into `buf` at `o`:
the integer part, then `k` fraction digits; returns the end. At most 18 bytes.
exports.summary: Writes `m / 10^k` (`m` below 10^15) with a `-` when `neg` and `m` is not 0 into `buf` at `o`: the integer part, then `k` fraction digits; returns the end.

exports.name: writeString
exports.signature: function writeString(out: string, s: string): void
exports.doc: Appends `s` as a quoted, escaped JSON string literal, as `JSON.stringify(s)` writes it.
exports.summary: Appends `s` as a quoted, escaped JSON string literal, as `JSON.stringify(s)` writes it.

exports.name: nextEscape
exports.signature: function nextEscape(s: string, from: usize, n: usize): usize
exports.doc:
The first byte of `s` from `from` to `n` (its length, or the end of a range of whole
characters within it) that needs escaping, or `n`. Sixteen bytes at a time: a block stops the
scan at its first byte below 0x20, `"` or `\`, or 0xED (the lead byte of U+D000–U+DFFF) with
0xA0 or above next (the bytes after the block's as a second vector), so Hangul and the rest of
U+D000–U+D7FF stay in the vector loop and only a lone surrogate stops it. The bytes after the
last whole block are read as the range's last sixteen (those already checked are clean); in
that block, 0xED is checked byte by byte. Shorter ranges are checked byte by byte. (The 0xED
check and the last block come from #1066.)
exports.summary: The first byte of `s` from `from` to `n` (its length, or the end of a range of whole characters within it) that needs escaping, or `n`.

exports.name: copyRun
exports.signature: function copyRun(buf: u8[], o: usize, s: string, start: usize, end: usize, n: usize): usize
exports.doc:
Copies bytes `start` to `end` of `s` (`n` bytes) to `buf` at `o`; the position after them.
Whole blocks while sixteen bytes of `s` are left (the last may run up to 15 bytes past `end`
in `buf`: room the caller keeps, and overwrites later), then byte by byte.
exports.summary: Copies bytes `start` to `end` of `s` (`n` bytes) to `buf` at `o`; the position after them.

modules.doc:
std/jsx/escape: HTML escaping of text and attributes (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md
"Escaping").

Text and attribute values escape `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` as react-dom does: like std/html
`escapeHtml`, but `'` is `'` (`velt_rt_jsx_escape`, one pass in the runtime). The compiler
escapes static text and attributes of precompiled templates the same way, and leaves those with a
`'` to `jsxEscape`/`jsxAttr`, so both lowerings render the same bytes.
modules.summary: std/jsx/escape: HTML escaping of text and attributes (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md "Escaping").

modules.doc:
std/jsx/factory: the functions compiled JSX calls (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md "Required
exports" and "SSR precompile"), plus `raw`. Internal: std/jsx/jsx-runtime re-exports them.

Every factory renders what it can at once (node.vlt): text is escaped into the new node's strings
and child nodes become its slots, and a child that still waits for an async component is kept as
a part, with the markup after it collected in a following complete part.
modules.summary: std/jsx/factory: the functions compiled JSX calls (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md "Required exports" and "SSR precompile"), plus `raw`.

exports.name: jsxComponent
exports.signature: function jsxComponent<P, E>(component: (props: P) => Element throws E, props: P, key: string | null, name: string): Element
exports.doc:
`<Card …/>`: std/jsx has no context to set up, so it calls the component at once. What the
component throws does not propagate from here: the node then fails when it is rendered, with
a `RenderError` naming the component, like an async component's rejection. `name`
(`"<module path>#<Name>"`) is for providers that emit hydration markers; std/jsx renders none.
exports.summary: `<Card …/>`: std/jsx has no context to set up, so it calls the component at once.

exports.doc:
`<Posts …/>` for an async component: calls it now, so siblings load concurrently, and keeps
its promise in the node; rendering awaits it in document order, and a rejection surfaces then
as a `RenderError` naming the component.
exports.summary: `<Posts …/>` for an async component: calls it now, so siblings load concurrently, and keeps its promise in the node; rendering awaits it in document order, and a rejection surfaces then as a `RenderError` naming the component.

generic, so the component's own error type cannot travel through the tree: its value is

modules.doc:
std/jsx/node: the value every JSX expression evaluates to (internal; std/jsx and
std/jsx/jsx-runtime export it).

std/jsx renders eagerly: building an element renders it, so a tree without async components
is its markup by the time it is complete. Text and attributes are escaped as they arrive. A
complete node is either one string (`html`), or the strings and child nodes of a template
(`tree`: `strings[0] slots[0] strings[1] … strings[n]`): a template, fragment or element keeps the
arrays its children came in, as JSX moves them there, instead of copying their markup. The
markup is copied once, when the tree is rendered into one string or written into a response
(`markupOf`, `writeMarkup`).

Only an async component cannot be rendered up front: its node holds the component's started
promise, and every node above it keeps its finished markup in `html` plus the rest, in order,
in `rest.parts` (a component that threw is kept the same way, as a node that fails when
rendered). The renderer (render.vlt) writes `html`, then awaits `rest.pending`, then renders
`rest.parts`, so markup before a pending component can be sent while it still loads.
modules.summary: std/jsx/node: the value every JSX expression evaluates to (internal; std/jsx and std/jsx/jsx-runtime export it).

std/jsx/render: turns an Element into HTML, as one string or as a streamed response body.

A complete element already is its HTML, as a string or a tree of template strings (node.vlt)
joined or written once. Otherwise the renderer walks the node's
pieces in document order with an explicit stack (no async recursion): `html`, then the
awaited async component, then the other parts. Every async component started when its node was
created, so awaiting them one after the other still lets them load concurrently.

objects and class instances (and structs or unions holding any) do; numbers, `bool` and
SIMD vectors do not. The same for every value of a type, and a constant where the type is
known, so `if (needsDrop(x))` costs nothing: a generic container can skip bookkeeping that
only matters for values that hold memory (Rust's `std::mem::needs_drop`).

blank, and one without a blank value gives the value itself (`hasBlank()` is false), which a
container then replaces when that value goes. A type implements `Blank` to give one.

modules.doc:
std/net: TCP, and TLS over TCP, over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md
§6). A TLS connection (`connectTls`, a `listenTls` listener) is a `TcpStream` like any other.

Handles: the runtime's `VeltListener` / `VeltStream` are opaque `u64` handles (rt_abi_async.md
§3.2), declared and defined as `u64` on every target.
`TcpListener` and `TcpStream` are Copy structs around that handle, like file descriptors:
- async methods take `this` by copy, so `await conn.readString()` never moves `conn` and a
  listener can be moved into a spawned task while its `port` is still read outside;
- the handle is released only by `close()`: an unclosed handle leaks until process exit. The
  handle is a key into a runtime table, not an address: after `close()` through any copy,
  every copy is dead: its operations throw `IoError` `EBADF` ("handle is closed") and closing
  again does nothing. They cannot use a `[Symbol.dispose]()` drop hook: a type with one is never Copy,
  and an async method owns (moves) its `this`, so `await conn.readString(); await
  conn.write(...)` would not compile. The runtime keeps a socket alive while an operation is
  in flight, so `close()` may be called at any time.
modules.summary: std/net: TCP, and TLS over TCP, over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §6).

exports.summary: A bound listening socket.

members.doc:

handshake runs with the stream's first read or write, which throws if it fails (10 s limit).
members.summary: Waits for the next connection (TCP_NODELAY is on).

members.name: close
members.doc:
Releases the handle: later `accept`s through any copy throw `IoError` `EBADF`, and closing
again does nothing. An `accept` already waiting keeps the socket open until it completes.
members.summary: Releases the handle: later `accept`s through any copy throw `IoError` `EBADF`, and closing again does nothing.

exports.name: TcpStream
exports.doc: A connected TCP stream.
exports.summary: A connected TCP stream.

members.name: read
members.doc: The next 1..max bytes (`max == 0`: up to 64 KiB); an empty array means end of stream.
members.summary: The next 1..max bytes (`max == 0`: up to 64 KiB); an empty array means end of stream.

members.name: readString
members.doc:
The next chunk as UTF-8 (a character split across reads is completed by the next call,
invalid bytes become U+FFFD); "" means end of stream.
members.summary: The next chunk as UTF-8 (a character split across reads is completed by the next call, invalid bytes become U+FFFD); "" means end of stream.

members.name: readInto
members.doc:
Reads what has arrived into `buf`, at most `buf.length` bytes, straight from the socket
(nothing is allocated or copied on the way for a plain TCP stream): the number of bytes
read, or `null` at the end of the stream (as Deno's `conn.read`). Waits only when nothing
has arrived yet. An empty `buf` reads nothing and returns 0. Reusing one buffer per
connection, and `subarray` views of what was read, keeps a server from copying its input.
members.summary: Reads what has arrived into `buf`, at most `buf.length` bytes, straight from the socket (nothing is allocated or copied on the way for a plain TCP stream): the number of bytes read, or `null` at the end of the stream (as Deno's `conn.read`).

members.name: tryRead
members.signature: tryRead(buf: u8[] | Uint8Array, start: number = 0, end?: number): number | null
members.doc:
Reads what has arrived into `buf[start..end]` without waiting: the number of bytes read,
`0` when nothing has arrived yet (`await readable()`, then try again), or `null` at the end
of the stream. A plain TCP stream reads straight into `buf`, so a parser can read into its
own buffer with nothing allocated or copied (`readInto` does the waiting for a
`Uint8Array`). `RangeError` for an empty or out-of-range range.
members.summary: Reads what has arrived into `buf[start..end]` without waiting: the number of bytes read, `0` when nothing has arrived yet (`await readable()`, then try again), or `null` at the end of the stream.

members.name: readable

members.doc:

everything else it queued until then: one system call where a write each would make
several, and nothing held back past a wait. Returns the number of bytes still to be sent on
this stream; `await drained(max)` keeps that bounded. A `write` goes after what was queued
before it. Throws `IoError` once sending failed (the error a `write` would have reported),
the stream was aborted or the handle closed.

modules.doc:
std/postgres: a PostgreSQL client (tokio-postgres in the runtime; rt_abi_async.md §14.13),
with an API close to node-postgres: `connect(url)` for one connection, `createPool({ url,
max })` for many. Every server round trip is async.

Parameters are a value `P` that std turns into JSON: an array binds `$1, $2, …` by
position; an object binds `:name` / `$name` placeholders by field name (std rewrites them
to `$n` once per statement; `::type` casts, strings, quoted identifiers and comments are
left alone). Values are converted for the parameter types the server inferred: numbers for
integer, float, numeric and text parameters (integers are range-checked), bools for `bool`,
`u8[]` for `bytea`, strings for text and json types, and a string in PostgreSQL's input
syntax for anything else (`uuid`, `date`, `timestamptz`, arrays like "{1,2}" …). Use
`{}` or the `select` / `selectOne` / `run` forms for statements without parameters.

Rows are decoded with `JSON.parse<T[]>`: each column fills the field of the same name
(rename with `AS`). int2/int4/int8 → exact integers, float4/float8 → `f64`, numeric → its
exact digits as a `string` (cast `::float8` for a number), bool → `bool`, text types, enums
and uuid → `string`, date/time/timestamp/timestamptz → ISO 8601 `string` (timestamptz in UTC
with "Z"), interval, inet/cidr and macaddr → PostgreSQL's text form as a `string`, money →
its exact amount as a `string`, json/jsonb → the document (any matching `T`), bytea → `u8[]`,
arrays → `T[]`, domains → as their base type, NULL → `T | null` fields. Other types (ranges,
composites, geometric types …) throw "ENOTSUP": cast them.

`batchQuery` / `batchQueryOne` / `batchExecute` run one statement with many parameter sets
in one round trip: one message group with a single Sync (what pgx's Batch does), so the
server runs them as one implicit transaction. When one execution fails, the server skips the
rest: the whole batch throws that error, and outside a transaction its writes are all or
nothing.

`Client` and `Pool` are Copy handles like std/net's sockets: pass and capture them freely
(also into spawned tasks: a client pipelines concurrent queries, a pool runs them on
separate connections) and release them once with `close()` / `end()`.
modules.summary: std/postgres: a PostgreSQL client (tokio-postgres in the runtime; rt_abi_async.md §14.13), with an API close to node-postgres: `connect(url)` for one connection, `createPool({ url, max })` for many.

exports.name: PgError
exports.doc:
A failed PostgreSQL operation. `code` is the server's SQLSTATE ("23505" unique violation,
"42P01" undefined table, "42601" syntax error, "25P02" aborted transaction …) or, for
failures outside the server: "ECONNREFUSED" and the other std/io names, "ECONNRESET" (the
connection was lost), "ECLOSED" (closed client or ended pool), "EINVAL" (bad connection
string or parameters), "ETLS" (TLS handshake or certificate), "ENOTSUP" (a column type
that cannot be decoded) or "EMISMATCH" (a row that does not fit the requested type).
exports.summary: A failed PostgreSQL operation.

Up to `max` connections, opened on demand and reused. `query` & co. borrow a connection
for one statement; `connect()` and `transaction` keep one for longer.
exports.summary: Up to `max` connections, opened on demand and reused.

exports.name: connect
exports.doc:
Connects to the server at `url`: "postgres://user:password@host:port/database?options"
or a libpq "host=… user=… dbname=…" string. `sslmode` is disable, prefer (default),
require (encrypted, certificate not checked), verify-ca or verify-full (Mozilla's roots
plus the PEM file named by `sslrootcert`). Throws `PgError`.
exports.summary: Connects to the server at `url`: "postgres://user:password@host:port/database?options" or a libpq "host=… user=… dbname=…" string.

exports.doc: A pool for `opts.url` (connections open on first use; a bad connection string throws now).

modules.doc:
Prelude: JS-style methods on every array `T[]` (implicitly imported into every module).

Conventions (see std/README.md):
- Callbacks are non-escaping function params; elements are passed to them as borrows, so
  iterating never copies non-Copy elements. Like JS, they also get the element's index (a
  callback may take fewer parameters: `xs.map((x) => …)`). A callback may throw: the method throws what its
  callback throws (`E`, inferred per call; `never` when the callback cannot throw).
- A callback may change the array through another reference (an alias, or an object holding
  it). Lowering passes a share of the element instead of a borrow when the array is one
  other references may reach (velt_vir stabilize.rs), so the argument stays valid when a
  push moves the buffer or a `pop` drops the element. The methods visit the indices below
  the length they started with, and stop at the length the callback leaves when it is
  shorter: `forEach`, `filter`, `reduce`, `some` and `every` skip the missing indices as JS
  does; JS's `find` family visits them with `undefined`, which a `T` cannot be; `map`, whose
  JS result would have holes, panics. `__intrinsic_may_alias(this)` is a constant, false when
  no other reference to an array of this type can exist: the length cannot change then, and
  the plain loop on `this.length` is all that is compiled. Otherwise the loop compares the
  index with one bound `n`, lowered after a callback shortened the array.
- Methods that return elements *out of* the array (`find`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`) return
  the elements themselves, like JS: objects are shared (another reference to the same object,
  a count increment), numbers, bool and strings are copied.
- Indices are `usize` internally; positions reported to users (`indexOf`, `findIndex`) are
  `i64` with -1 for "absent", like JS.
- Sorting (`sort()`, `sort(cmp)`) lives in sort.vlt. `clone()` (a deep copy) is compiler-provided.
modules.summary: Prelude: JS-style methods on every array `T[]` (implicitly imported into every module).

members.name: slice
members.doc:
The elements in [start, end), themselves (objects are shared, as in JS). JS semantics:
negative positions count from the end, out-of-range positions are clamped, and `end`
defaults to the length.
members.summary: The elements in [start, end), themselves (objects are shared, as in JS).

members.summary: New array with this array's elements followed by `other`'s.

members.name: swap
members.doc:
Exchanges elements `i` and `j` (each must be below the length): their bits change places,
nothing is copied or dropped.
members.summary: Exchanges elements `i` and `j` (each must be below the length): their bits change places, nothing is copied or dropped.

members.name: rotateLeft
members.doc:
Rotates the elements in `[start, end)` one place down: the one at `start` moves to `end - 1`
and the others one place towards `start`, by one memory move (what `splice` would do with
a removal and an insert). `end` must be at most the length, `start` at most `end`.
members.summary: Rotates the elements in `[start, end)` one place down: the one at `start` moves to `end - 1` and the others one place towards `start`, by one memory move (what `splice` would do with a removal and an insert).

members.name: rotateRight
members.doc: As `rotateLeft`, one place up: the element at `end - 1` moves to `start`.
members.summary: As `rotateLeft`, one place up: the element at `end - 1` moves to `start`.

members.name: prefetch
members.doc:
A hint that element `i` is read soon: the CPU starts loading it, so that the read does not
wait for memory (a hint only, it changes nothing; an index past the end does nothing).
members.summary: A hint that element `i` is read soon: the CPU starts loading it, so that the read does not wait for memory (a hint only, it changes nothing; an index past the end does nothing).

members.name: reserve
members.doc: Makes room for `extra` more elements without growing again (the length stays).
members.summary: Makes room for `extra` more elements without growing again (the length stays).

members.name: reverse
members.doc: Reverses in place (JS also returns the array; here the result is `void`, see `fill`).
members.summary: Reverses in place (JS also returns the array; here the result is `void`, see `fill`).

members.name: splice
members.signature: splice(start: i64, deleteCount: i64 = 9223372036854775807, ... items: T[] = ): T[]
members.doc:
Removes `deleteCount` elements from `start` (positions as in `slice`; omitted: the rest),
inserts `items` there, and returns the removed elements, like JS. O(length).
members.summary: Removes `deleteCount` elements from `start` (positions as in `slice`; omitted: the rest), inserts `items` there, and returns the removed elements, like JS.

members.name: shift
members.doc:
Removes and returns the first element, or `undefined` when the array is empty.
O(length): the other elements move down by one, as V8 does for large arrays. A queue that
takes from the front belongs in a `Deque` (velt:collections/deque), which does it in O(1).
members.summary: Removes and returns the first element, or `undefined` when the array is empty.

members.name: unshift
members.doc:
Inserts `items` at the front, in order, and returns the new length, like JS. O(length +
items): the items are pushed, then rotated to the front by three reversals.
members.summary: Inserts `items` at the front, in order, and returns the new length, like JS.

members.name: truncate
members.doc:
Shortens the array to `length` elements, dropping the rest (JS `xs.length = n`); a longer
`length` leaves it unchanged. Panics on a negative `length`, like JS's RangeError.
members.summary: Shortens the array to `length` elements, dropping the rest (JS `xs.length = n`); a longer `length` leaves it unchanged.

members.name: length
members.doc:
The number of elements, for `xs.length -= k` and `xs.length--` (which set it through the
setter below); a plain read of `xs.length` compiles to the length itself.
members.summary: The number of elements, for `xs.length -= k` and `xs.length--` (which set it through the setter below); a plain read of `xs.length` compiles to the length itself.

members.name: length
members.doc:
`xs.length = n`, as in JS: drops the elements from `n` on (`xs.length = 0` empties the
array). A length that is not a whole number from 0 to 2^52 - 1, the most elements a Velt
array holds (JS stops at 2^32 - 1), panics with `RangeError: Invalid array length`
(`arrayLength`). A larger `n` than the array's length panics too: JS would add empty
slots, which Velt has no value for (push the elements, or build the array with
`new Array<T>(n).fill(v)`).
members.summary: `xs.length = n`, as in JS: drops the elements from `n` on (`xs.length = 0` empties the array).

members.doc: The elements in reverse order.
members.summary: The elements in reverse order.

members.doc:
`splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` on a copy: the array with the elements removed and
`items` inserted.
members.summary: `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` on a copy: the array with the elements removed and `items` inserted.

members.doc:
A copy with `value` at `index` (negative counts from the end). Panics like JS's RangeError

members.summary: A copy with `value` at `index` (negative counts from the end).

members.doc: Whether the array has no elements (`xs.length == 0`).
members.summary: Whether the array has no elements (`xs.length == 0`).

`[index, element]` pairs (see header). JS returns an iterator; an array

members.summary: `[index, element]` pairs (see header).

members.name: join
members.doc:
`join` for element types without their own (string enums, literal unions, objects): each
element as JS's `String(x)` writes an array element (a class instance through its
`toString()`, `[object Object]` for another object, `[object Map]` for a map). A struct
with its own `toString()`, an `Error` or a `RegExp` element is a compile error: write
`xs.map((x) => x.toString()).join(sep)`. Strings, numbers and bools have exact ones
below; arrays of arrays and of nullable elements have JS's in array_nested.vlt.
members.summary: `join` for element types without their own (string enums, literal unions, objects): each element as JS's `String(x)` writes an array element (a class instance through its `toString()`, `[object Object]` for another object, `[object Map]` for a map).

members.name: toString
members.doc:
The elements joined with ",", each as JS's `String(x)` writes an array element: what
`${xs}` writes (`[1, [2, 3], null].toString()` is `"1,2,3,"`).
members.summary: The elements joined with ",", each as JS's `String(x)` writes an array element: what `${xs}` writes (`[1, [2, 3], null].toString()` is `"1,2,3,"`).

members.name: join
members.doc:
Joins with `sep`: the runtime sums the lengths, then copies every piece once into a string
of exactly that size.
members.summary: Joins with `sep`: the runtime sums the lengths, then copies every piece once into a string of exactly that size.

`join` on numbers and booleans: each element is converted like `String(x)` (the same text
`console.log` prints), then joined as strings. One `extend` per element type, since a generic
`T` has no `toString`.
exports.summary: `join` on numbers and booleans: each element is converted like `String(x)` (the same text `console.log` prints), then joined as strings.

exports.name: __arrayFilled
exports.doc:
`new Array<T>(n).fill(v)` (the compiler rewrites it to this, `sema` `array_ctor`): `n` copies
of `v` in one allocation. `n` is a length as `xs.length = n` takes it (`arrayLength`):
`new Array(-1)`, `new Array(1.5)` and `new Array(NaN)` are a `RangeError`, as in Node.
exports.summary: `new Array<T>(n).fill(v)` (the compiler rewrites it to this, `sema` `array_ctor`): `n` copies of `v` in one allocation.

exports.name: __arrayOne
exports.signature: function __arrayOne<X, U>(_x: X, a: U): U
exports.doc:
`new Array<T>(x).fill(v)` with an `x` that is no number (sema `array_ctor`): as in JS, an
array of the one element `x`, which `fill` replaces with `v`. Sema passes `x` (evaluated
first, then dropped) and `[v]`.
exports.summary: `new Array<T>(x).fill(v)` with an `x` that is no number (sema `array_ctor`): as in JS, an array of the one element `x`, which `fill` replaces with `v`.

exports.doc: `Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => f(i))`: `f(i)` for each index, throwing what `f` throws.
exports.summary: `Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => f(i))`: `f(i)` for each index, throwing what `f` throws.

members.doc:
`this[index]` read where the program expects `T | undefined` (the compiler calls it, sema
`indexers.rs`): the element, or `undefined` when `index` is not a position in the array (out
of range, negative or not a whole number), as in JS.

modules.doc:
Prelude: `flat` on arrays of arrays, and `join` on arrays of arrays and of nullable elements,
like JS: inner arrays are written as `${x}` writes them (their elements joined with ",", at
any depth, `null` as ""), and `null` elements join as "". These targets are more specific
than `extend<T> Array<T>` (array.vlt), so their `join` wins.
modules.summary: Prelude: `flat` on arrays of arrays, and `join` on arrays of arrays and of nullable elements, like JS: inner arrays are written as `${x}` writes them (their elements joined with ",", at any depth, `null` as ""), and `null` elements join as "".

members.name: swapIn
members.signature: swapIn(a: usize, i: usize, b: usize, j: usize)
members.doc:
Exchanges `this[a][i]` and `this[b][j]` (every index must be in range), also between two

modules.doc:
Prelude: Node `Buffer`-style bulk operations on byte arrays (`u8[]`): short searches and XOR
masking sixteen bytes at a time with SIMD vectors, here in Velt so that they are compiled into
their caller; long searches by memchr, copying and filling by memmove and memset in the
runtime.

A byte array is a plain `u8[]` (Velt has no separate `Uint8Array` type), so every array
method works on it too; the methods here replace the generic ones of the same name for `u8[]`.
`Buffer.alloc(n)` makes a zeroed array in one allocation (calloc: large arrays cost no
memset). Positions follow JS: negative ones count from the end.
modules.summary: Prelude: Node `Buffer`-style bulk operations on byte arrays (`u8[]`): short searches and XOR masking sixteen bytes at a time with SIMD vectors, here in Velt so that they are compiled into their caller; long searches by memchr, copying and filling by memmove and memset in the runtime.

after every other value (and equal to itself), the total order `sort()` uses.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the JS `Date` object. An instant as milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, held as a
number (NaN for an invalid date), with JS's conventions: months are 0-11, the plain getters and
setters are local time (the OS time zone, DST-aware) and the `UTC` ones are UTC, and strings
parse like `Date.parse` (a date alone is UTC, a date-time without an offset is local time).
The calendar arithmetic is velt:datetime's; prefer its `DateTime` (UTC-first, months 1-12) in
new code.

Differences from JS: `toString()` has no time zone name in parentheses, and the `toLocale…`
methods always use the `en-US` format.
modules.summary: Prelude: the JS `Date` object.

exports.name: Date
exports.doc:
Enables basic storage and retrieval of dates and times: an instant in milliseconds since
1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, NaN for an invalid date, with JS's conventions (months 0-11, local-time
and UTC getters and setters). Prefer `velt:datetime`'s `DateTime` in new code.
exports.summary: Enables basic storage and retrieval of dates and times: an instant in milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, NaN for an invalid date, with JS's conventions (months 0-11, local-time and UTC getters and setters).

seconds?, ms?)` local time, with month 0-11 and fields rolling over like JS; a year of 0-99
means 1900-1999.

modules.doc:
Prelude: `Error`, the base class of every error thrown by std (`IoError`, `JsonError`).

A function's error type is the union of what it can throw, so a call that can fail in two ways
(e.g. `Response.json()` of a fetch: I/O, then JSON decoding) throws `IoError | JsonError`, and
`catch (e) { e.message }` works either way (every member has `message`). User error classes
extend it too.
modules.summary: Prelude: `Error`, the base class of every error thrown by std (`IoError`, `JsonError`).

exports.name: JSON
exports.doc:
Converts values to and from the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. Unlike JS, it is
typed: `stringify` and `parse` are generated for the static type at compile time, `parse<T>`
checks the text against `T` and throws `JsonError` instead of returning `any`. There is no
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)` until #924; `JSON.parseValue(text).revive(reviver)` does what it
does. `stringify` takes JS's `replacer` (an array of
keys, `null`, or a `JsonReplacer` function) and its `space`. `parseValue` reads a document
of any shape.
exports.summary: Converts values to and from the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format.

(`a?: string`) fails the decode, as a value of another type does (JavaScript would give the

exports.name: JsonParseOptions
exports.signature: type JsonParseOptions = { unknownKeys?: "ignore" | "reject"; maxDepth?: i64; comments?: "error" | "skip"; trailingCommas?: bool }
exports.doc:
Options of `JSON.parse<T>(text, options)`; every field may be left out.
- `unknownKeys`: "reject" makes an object key the target type has no field for an error,
  `unknown field at $.key` (default "ignore": it is skipped).
- `maxDepth`: the deepest nesting of arrays and objects allowed (default 128, like serde_json:
  a typed decoder recurses per level, so a much higher limit can overflow the stack).
- `comments`: "skip" reads line (`//`) and block comments as whitespace (JSONC, as in
  `tsconfig.json`; default "error").
- `trailingCommas`: true accepts a comma before `]` and `}` (JSONC; default false).
exports.summary: Options of `JSON.parse<T>(text, options)`; every field may be left out.

value to write there, or `undefined` to leave a member out (an array element is then `null`).
exports.summary: A replacer function of `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)`: called with each key and the JSON form of its value (the value passed itself under the key `""` first), it returns the value to write there, or `undefined` to leave a member out (an array element is then `null`).

exports.name: JsonValue
exports.doc:
A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt:json` calls it `Value`). It
has value semantics: an edit never shows through a clone, a parent or a child. Accessors on
the wrong kind return null / 0. `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse<T>` read and write it. Only
std makes one: the constructor is private, so no class can extend `JsonValue`.

Two forms (#1660). A parsed value is a position on a tape (velt:json/tape): reading it makes
nothing, and its children share the tape. A value built or edited here (`object()`, `set`, …)
or read from a database driver is a tree of reference-counted runtime nodes behind `#handle`
(which stays the first field: compiled glue writes it); an edit turns a tape value into such
a tree first, so it never shows through the tape.
exports.summary: A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt:json` calls it `Value`).

`replacement` expands `$&`, `$1`…`$99`, `$<name>`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$$`. A sticky regex
matches only at `lastIndex` (with `g`: from 0, each match where the previous one ended), and
`lastIndex` changes as in JS.

exports.name: UnderlyingSource
exports.doc:
What a `ReadableStream` reads from (JS's underlying source). `start(controller)` runs when the
stream is made, `pull(controller)` whenever the stream wants more chunks (it enqueues them, or
closes the stream), and `cancel(reason)` when a consumer cancels it. Each may be `async`, and
an error it throws errors the stream.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the iteration protocol (docs/reference/control-flow.md "for...of").

`for (const x of src)` works on arrays, on `Map`s and other classes with `entries()`, and on
any `Iterable<T, E>`: it calls `src[Symbol.iterator]()` once, then `next()` until a result
is `done`, and calls the iterator's `return()` when the loop is left early (`break`,
`return`, a thrown error). `E` is what `next()` throws (`never`: nothing); the loop throws
it too. Velt has no `undefined`, so a finished result has no `value` (reading `r.value`
without narrowing gives `T | null`).
modules.summary: Prelude: the iteration protocol (docs/reference/control-flow.md "for...of").

exports.signature: type IteratorResult<T> = { value: T; done: false } | { done: true }

One step of an iterator: `{ value, done: false }` for the next value, `{ done: true }` once it
is finished (Velt has no `undefined`: a finished result has no `value`).
exports.summary: One step of an iterator: `{ value, done: false }` for the next value, `{ done: true }` once it is finished (Velt has no `undefined`: a finished result has no `value`).

exports.name: Iterator
exports.doc:
Produces values one at a time with `next()` (`E`: what `next()` throws). `for...of` gets one

exports.signature: class AsyncGenerator<T, E = never> implements AsyncIterator<T, E>, AsyncIterable<T, E>, AsyncIterableIterator<T, E>
exports.doc:
An async generator (`async function*`, docs/reference/functions.md "Async generators"): what
calling one creates. Each `next()` runs the body up to its next `yield`, awaiting what the body
awaits on the way; its promise rejects with what the body throws (`E`). `return()` closes a
generator suspended at a `yield`: its `finally` blocks run (and may `await`) and its `using`
/ `await using` values are disposed, as if the `yield` were a `return`. Dropping it closes it
too, without awaiting: cleanup that would `await` is then cancelled (drops only), like a
cancelled async function. After it finished, threw, or was closed, `next()` reports `done`.

Like JS, `next()` and `return()` calls are queued: a call made while another one is still
running waits for its turn, so each promise settles with its own step, in call order. A call
whose promise nobody awaits still takes its turn (its value is dropped).

The compiler creates these objects: the generator's state follows the class's fields, and the
queue fields start at zero.
exports.summary: An async generator (`async function*`, docs/reference/functions.md "Async generators"): what calling one creates.

modules.doc:
Prelude, loaded on use: `JSON`, `JsonError` and `JsonValue` (rt_abi_async.md §12.3–12.5). A
program loads this module when one of its modules names one of them (the global
std/prelude/global/json.vlt) or imports a std module that uses them.

`JSON.stringify<T>` / `JSON.parse<T>` are compile-time generated per type by the compiler
intrinsics (a string builder for stringify, a pull-reader decoder for parse); parse failures
throw a `SyntaxError` `JsonError` ("expected string at $.name"). The stringify glue writes a
`JsonValue` (at any depth) with its private `__writeJson(b)`, decodes one with
`__fromReader(r)`, and `console.log` prints one from the runtime tree `__runtimeHandle()`
makes for it (freed after).

`JSON.parseValue` gives a `JsonValue` for data of unknown shape: a position on a tape (one
flat array per document, velt:json/tape), which its children share. A value built or edited
here is a tree of reference-counted runtime nodes behind an opaque `u64` handle
(rt_abi_async.md §3.2; 0 is the null handle, which a `JsonValue` holds for JSON null); an edit
turns a tape value into such a tree first.
Values have value semantics: `set`/`delete`/`push`/`setAt` copy a node another handle shares
before changing it (copy-on-write), so an edit never shows through a clone, a parent or a
child. Every `JsonValue` owns one reference to its tape or tree (`get`/`at`/`clone` return
new ones; children stay valid after their parent is released); a tree's is released by the
`[Symbol.dispose]()` drop hook. A value that contains a `JsonValue` has no automatic deep
`clone()` (sema rejects it: the generated copy could not take a new reference).
modules.summary: Prelude, loaded on use: `JSON`, `JsonError` and `JsonValue` (rt_abi_async.md §12.3–12.5).

- `unknownKeys`: "reject" makes an object key the target type has no field for an error,
  `unknown field at $.key` (default "ignore": it is skipped).
- `maxDepth`: the deepest nesting of arrays and objects allowed (default 128, like serde_json:
  a typed decoder recurses per level, so a much higher limit can overflow the stack).
- `comments`: "skip" reads line (`//`) and block comments as whitespace (JSONC, as in
  `tsconfig.json`; default "error").
- `trailingCommas`: true accepts a comma before `]` and `}` (JSONC; default false).

exports.doc:
A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt:json` calls it `Value`). It
has value semantics: an edit never shows through a clone, a parent or a child. Accessors on
the wrong kind return null / 0. `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse<T>` read and write it. Only
std makes one: the constructor is private, so no class can extend `JsonValue`.

Two forms (#1660). A parsed value is a position on a tape (velt:json/tape): reading it makes
nothing, and its children share the tape. A value built or edited here (`object()`, `set`, …)
or read from a database driver is a tree of reference-counted runtime nodes behind `#handle`
(which stays the first field: compiled glue writes it); an edit turns a tape value into such
a tree first, so it never shows through the tape.

modules.doc:
Prelude: `Map<K, V>`, an insertion-ordered hash map with JS `Map` semantics.

Layout (like CPython's dict / indexmap):
- Entries live in two dense parallel arrays (`entryKeys`, `entryValues`) in insertion order,
  so iteration is a linear scan and order matches JS. A deleted entry's value is dropped at
  once (set to null); its key stays as a tombstone until the next compaction. (One array of
  `{ key, value }` entries measured ~20% slower on k-nucleotide: probing reads only keys, and
  they pack densest on their own. Values stay `V | null` so a delete drops the value at once.)
- A null value marks a deleted entry only where `V` excludes null. When `V` includes null
  (`Map<string, number | null>`, a `Record<string, T | null>`), `V | null` is `V` and a live
  entry may hold null too: such an entry is live when the map has no tombstones (`dead == 0`,
  the common case) or a slot of the index points at it (a delete removes the entry's slot at
  once, its key stays). `__intrinsic_holds_null` is a constant per instantiation, so maps
  whose `V` excludes null keep this layout and code unchanged (no extra field, no per-entry
  flag). Maps whose `V` includes null pay only while they have tombstones: `keys()`,
  `values()`, `entries()`, `compact` and the other bulk readers then mark the live positions
  from the slot words in one pass (`liveBits`), and `forEach`, `for...of` and the formatting
  and JSON glue probe the index for each null-valued entry, deleted ones included (`liveNull`).
- `slots` is an open-addressing index (power-of-two capacity) of packed `u64` words:
  the top 32 bits of the entry's scrambled hash `p = hash * 2^64/phi` (Fibonacci hashing,
  which spreads even weak hashes such as sequential integers), and in the low 32 bits the
  entry position + 1 (0 = empty slot). The home slot of `p` is its top bits, so the stored
  tag also gives every slot's home: probing rejects most non-matching slots without loading
  the key, and growing or deleting never rehashes keys.
- Collisions use Robin Hood linear probing: every probe cluster is kept sorted by home slot,
  so a lookup stops at the first slot whose resident is closer to its own home than the key
  would be (misses are short even at high load), inserts shift the rest of the cluster one
  slot right, and deletes shift it back (no tombstones in the index). The index grows at 3/4
  load (as fast as plain linear probing grown at 5/8 in bench/hashmap.vlt, with half the
  index memory at some sizes; bench/RESULTS.md).

Ownership: `set` takes ownership of the key and value. `get` returns the stored value like JS
(an object is shared — another reference to it — and numbers or strings are copied); `upsert`
/ `update` change a value in place. `keys()`, `values()` and `entries()` return the stored
keys and values the same way; `forEach` borrows. A map holds at most 2^31 entries.

Live iteration (JS order: entries added while a loop runs are visited, deleted ones are not):
`forEach` and `for...of` over a map (or its `keys()`, `values()`, `entries()`, through a
`MapCursor`) walk the entry positions. A compaction, the pop of the newest entry and clearing
renumber positions; they alone bump `renumbers`, and a loop that sees it changed finds its
place again by *sequence number*: every entry has one, increasing in insertion order and never
reused. The sequence number of the entry at position `p` is `p + off`, with `off` from the
last breakpoint at or before `p` in (`seqPos`, `seqOff`); a map that never renumbered has no
breakpoints (`off` is 0). Renumbering rebuilds the breakpoints (at most one per run of
removed entries), so set, get and append never touch them.
modules.summary: Prelude: `Map<K, V>`, an insertion-ordered hash map with JS `Map` semantics.

exports.name: Map
exports.doc:
A collection of key/value pairs that remembers insertion order, with JS `Map` semantics:
re-setting a key keeps its position, and float keys compare like JS (`NaN` finds itself, `0`
and `-0` are one key). Numbers, `bool` and strings compare by value; objects (class instances,
object types, arrays, maps, records, interface and function values) by identity, as in JS, so
a key changed in place keeps its entry. Unlike JS, tuples compare part by part, as `===` does
(a tuple key is hashed when inserted: don't change it while it is in a map).
exports.summary: A collection of key/value pairs that remembers insertion order, with JS `Map` semantics: re-setting a key keeps its position, and float keys compare like JS (`NaN` finds itself, `0` and `-0` are one key).

members.name: constructor
members.doc:
A map holding `entries` (like JS `new Map(entries)`), in order; a later entry with the same
key replaces the value of an earlier one but keeps its position. Leaves `entries` as it is;
the map shares their keys and values, like JS. `new Map(iterable)` also takes any iterable
of pairs (a generator, another map), which the compiler collects into an array first.
members.summary: A map holding `entries` (like JS `new Map(entries)`), in order; a later entry with the same key replaces the value of an earlier one but keeps its position.

members.name: size
members.doc: Number of entries (like JS `Map.prototype.size`).
members.summary: Number of entries (like JS `Map.prototype.size`).

members.name: set
members.doc:
Inserts or replaces. On replace the new key is dropped and the entry keeps its position
(JS semantics: re-setting a key does not move it to the end).
members.summary: Inserts or replaces.

members.name: get
members.doc:
The value stored for `key`, or `undefined` when it has none. Like JS it is the stored value
itself: an object is shared (another reference to it), a number or string is copied.
members.summary: The value stored for `key`, or `undefined` when it has none.

members.name: __at
members.doc:
The value stored for `key`, which is present (a literal-key `Record` reads its keys with it);
unlike `get(key)!` it reads a live entry holding null as that null.
members.summary: The value stored for `key`, which is present (a literal-key `Record` reads its keys with it); unlike `get(key)!` it reads a live entry holding null as that null.

members.name: has
members.doc: Whether the map has an entry for `key`, matched as `get` matches it.
members.summary: Whether the map has an entry for `key`, matched as `get` matches it.

members.name: upsert
members.signature: upsert<E>(key: K, init: V, f: (value: V) => V throws E) throws E
members.summary: If `key` is present, replaces its value with `f(value)` (which borrows the old value); otherwise inserts `init` (dropped unused when `key` is present).

members.name: update
members.signature: update<E>(key: K, f: (value: V) => void throws E): bool throws E
members.doc:
Calls `f` with the value stored for `key` (not a copy), so an object value can be changed
in place: `m.update(k, (xs) => { xs.push(x); })`. Values that copy (numbers, `bool`,
strings) arrive as copies, like any such argument: replace them with `upsert` or `set`.
Returns whether `key` was present.
members.summary: Calls `f` with the value stored for `key` (not a copy), so an object value can be changed in place: `m.update(k, (xs) => { xs.push(x); })`.

members.signature: getOrInsert<E>(key: K, make: () => V throws E): V throws E
members.doc: The value stored for `key`, inserting `make()` first if `key` is absent.
members.summary: The value stored for `key`, inserting `make()` first if `key` is absent.

members.name: delete
members.doc: Removes `key`; returns whether it was present. The value is dropped immediately.
members.summary: Removes `key`; returns whether it was present.

members.name: clear
members.doc: Removes all entries.
members.summary: Removes all entries.

members.name: keys
members.doc:
Returns the keys in the map, in insertion order. JS returns an iterator; this is an array of
the keys there are now. `for (const k of m.keys())` iterates live instead, as in JS: it
visits keys added while it runs and skips deleted ones.
members.summary: Returns the keys in the map, in insertion order.

members.name: __markNullProto
members.doc: Marks this map as a prototype-less record's entries (`Object.create(null)`).
members.summary: Marks this map as a prototype-less record's entries (`Object.create(null)`).

members.summary: Was this map marked by `__markNullProto`?

Whether the newest entry's key starts with a digit (a `Record` key that may be an array

members.summary: The positions of the live entries in `entryKeys` / `entryValues` (a record's glue).

members.doc:
Returns the values in the map, in insertion order (an array; JS returns an iterator).

members.signature: forEach<E>(f: (value: V, key: K) => void throws E) throws E
members.doc:
Visits the entries in insertion order, borrowing them (JS argument order: value, key). As in
JS, entries `f` adds are visited too and entries it deletes are not.
members.summary: Visits the entries in insertion order, borrowing them (JS argument order: value, key).

members.doc: A cursor before the first entry, for `__advance`.
members.summary: A cursor before the first entry, for `__advance`.

members.name: __advance
members.doc:
Moves `c` to the next entry (in insertion order, including entries added since the loop
started); false at the end.
members.summary: Moves `c` to the next entry (in insertion order, including entries added since the loop started); false at the end.

members.name: __valueAt
members.doc: The value of the entry `c` is at.
members.summary: The value of the entry `c` is at.

members.summary: The `[key, value]` pair of the entry `c` is at.

members.name: __deepEquals
members.doc:
`deepEqual` (the compiler's equality glue calls it): the same keys, matched as `get`
matches them, each with a deeply equal value, in any order (Node's `isDeepStrictEqual`).
`deep`: the values (and unmatched keys) compare as Vitest's `toEqual` does
(`__intrinsic_deep_eq`: class instances by their fields).
members.summary: `deepEqual` (the compiler's equality glue calls it): the same keys, matched as `get` matches them, each with a deeply equal value, in any order (Node's `isDeepStrictEqual`).

members.name: __liveAt
members.doc:
Whether entry position `e` holds a live entry, not a deleted one (the formatting and JSON
glue ask it for maps whose `V` includes null; for the others a null value answers).
members.summary: Whether entry position `e` holds a live entry, not a deleted one (the formatting and JSON glue ask it for maps whose `V` includes null; for the others a null value answers).

exports.name: Map<string, V>
exports.doc:
A map with string keys, looked up by the UTF-8 bytes of a key (Velt): a server reading keys
from the network finds them without making a string per request. Each method is the one
without `Utf8` called with the bytes decoded (`utf8DecodeLossy`: an invalid sequence reads as
U+FFFD); valid UTF-8 is hashed and compared as it is, and a string is made only to store a
new key.
exports.summary: A map with string keys, looked up by the UTF-8 bytes of a key (Velt): a server reading keys from the network finds them without making a string per request.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the JS `Math` object as a class of static constants and methods on f64.

Rounding and `sqrt`/`abs` map to single compiler intrinsics (one machine instruction on
x86_64/aarch64). `min`/`max` follow JS exactly: NaN if either operand is NaN, and
-0 < +0 (`Math.max(-0, 0)` is +0, `Math.min(0, -0)` is -0).
modules.summary: Prelude: the JS `Math` object as a class of static constants and methods on f64.

exports.name: Math
exports.doc:
Basic mathematics functionality and constants, on numbers (`f64`). Integers up to 32 bits
convert implicitly; a 64-bit integer does not: write `x as number`.
exports.summary: Basic mathematics functionality and constants, on numbers (`f64`).

members.name: PI
members.doc: Pi. This is the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter.
members.summary: Pi.

members.name: trunc
members.doc:
Returns the integral part of a numeric expression, `x`, removing any fractional digits.
If `x` is already an integer, the result is `x`. `Math.trunc(a / b)` with two integer
operands is integer division instead, and its result is an integer.

params.doc: A numeric expression.

members.doc:
Returns the absolute value of a number (the value without regard to whether it is positive or
negative).
For example, the absolute value of -5 is the same as the absolute value of 5.
members.summary: Returns the absolute value of a number (the value without regard to whether it is positive or negative).

params.name: x
params.doc: A numeric expression for which the absolute value is needed.

members.doc: -1, 0 or 1 with the sign of `x`; keeps -0 and NaN as they are, like JS.
members.summary: -1, 0 or 1 with the sign of `x`; keeps -0 and NaN as they are, like JS.

members.name: max
members.signature: static max(a: f64 = -Infinity, b: f64 = -Infinity, ... rest: f64[] = ): f64
members.doc:
Any number of values, like JS (`Math.max()` is -Infinity). A call with 2 to 16 plain
arguments compiles to a balanced tree of `max2` calls (sema, `body/expr/math_minmax.rs`)
and never builds the rest array; this body runs for spread calls and the other counts.
members.summary: Any number of values, like JS (`Math.max()` is -Infinity).

members.signature: static min(a: f64 = Infinity, b: f64 = Infinity, ... rest: f64[] = ): f64
members.doc:
Returns the smaller of a set of supplied numeric expressions: any number of values, like JS
(`Math.min()` is Infinity). NaN if any value is NaN. Calls with 2 to 16 plain arguments
compile to a tree of `min2` calls, as for `max`.
members.summary: Returns the smaller of a set of supplied numeric expressions: any number of values, like JS (`Math.min()` is Infinity).

members.name: random
members.doc:
Uniform in [0, 1), like JS: the per-thread generator of `velt:random` (not for secrets; use

members.doc: Returns the value of a base expression taken to a specified power.

members.name: hypot
members.doc:
sqrt(a² + b² + c² + …) without overflow or underflow: operands far from 1 are scaled by an
exact power of two (2^±600) first, so ordinary inputs stay correctly rounded. Any number of
values, like JS; past four they are scaled by the largest one. Infinity wins over NaN, like
JS.
members.summary: sqrt(a² + b² + c² + …) without overflow or underflow: operands far from 1 are scaled by an exact power of two (2^±600) first, so ordinary inputs stay correctly rounded.

members.name: imul
members.signature: static imul(a: f64, b: f64): i64
members.doc:
JS `Math.imul`: the low 32 bits of the product of ToInt32 of both operands. A call on
numbers compiles to one 32-bit multiply (sema `int32.rs`); this body serves function values.
members.summary: JS `Math.imul`: the low 32 bits of the product of ToInt32 of both operands.

members.name: clz32
members.doc: JS `Math.clz32`: leading zero bits of ToUint32 of `x` (32 for 0).
members.summary: JS `Math.clz32`: leading zero bits of ToUint32 of `x` (32 for 0).

members.name: umulh
members.signature: static umulh(a: u64, b: u64): u64
members.doc:
High 64 bits of the 128-bit product `a * b`, for 64-bit limb arithmetic (the low bits are
`a * b`, which wraps). Not in JS; like C#'s `Math.BigMul` / Rust's widening multiply.
members.summary: High 64 bits of the 128-bit product `a * b`, for 64-bit limb arithmetic (the low bits are `a * b`, which wraps).

exports.name: __mulToInt32
exports.doc:
ToInt32 of the product `a * b` of two JS numbers (`(y * k) | 0`; sema `int32.rs` inserts the
call). JS multiplies doubles, so a product past 2^53 is rounded before its low 32 bits are
taken. For int32 operands that is `velt_rt_math_mul_int32` (one multiply when `numrep` proves
the product within 2^53); other values multiply as doubles.
exports.summary: ToInt32 of the product `a * b` of two JS numbers (`(y * k) | 0`; sema `int32.rs` inserts the call).

exports.name: __floatIndex
exports.doc:
`xs[i]` with a float `i` (a JS number; the compiler inserts the call, `sema` `numbers.rs`): a
whole number indexes as usual. Anything else would read `undefined` in JS; here it panics like
an index out of bounds.
exports.summary: `xs[i]` with a float `i` (a JS number; the compiler inserts the call, `sema` `numbers.rs`): a whole number indexes as usual.

exports.name: __floatPosition
exports.doc:
A `number` given as a position or lane index of a SIMD method (the compiler inserts the call,
`sema` `numbers.rs`): a whole number from 0 up as itself. Anything else is the largest `usize`,
which is out of range everywhere, so `fits` gives `false` and the others a `RangeError`.
exports.summary: A `number` given as a position or lane index of a SIMD method (the compiler inserts the call, `sema` `numbers.rs`): a whole number from 0 up as itself.

so they consume it: `x.unwrapOr(d)` gives up `x`. The usual receivers are temporaries
(`find(xs, k).unwrapOr(0)`), where that is free. For Copy payloads the receiver stays usable.
`isNull` only borrows.

Prelude: JS number globals (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `isNaN`, `isFinite`), `toFixed`,
`toExponential` and `toPrecision` on f64, and
the static members of `Number` (`Number.isInteger`, `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, …).

exports.name: NaN
exports.doc:
A value that is not a number (an `f64`). NaN does not equal any value, including itself: test
for it with `isNaN(x)`.
exports.summary: A value that is not a number (an `f64`).

exports.name: Infinity
exports.doc: Positive infinity, an `f64` greater than every finite one. `-Infinity` is its negation.
exports.summary: Positive infinity, an `f64` greater than every finite one.

exports.name: isNaN
exports.doc: Whether `x` is NaN (JS global `isNaN` on a number).
exports.summary: Whether `x` is NaN (JS global `isNaN` on a number).

exports.name: isFinite
exports.doc: Whether `x` is neither NaN nor ±Infinity.
exports.summary: Whether `x` is neither NaN nor ±Infinity.

members.name: toFixed
members.doc:
`digits` (0 to 100) decimals, rounded like JS: to the nearest, and on an exact tie away from
zero (`(0.5).toFixed(0)` is "1", `(-1.25).toFixed(1)` is "-1.3"; `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is
"1.00" because 1.005 is really 1.00499…). From 1e21 up it is `String(x)`, as in JS.
members.summary: `digits` (0 to 100) decimals, rounded like JS: to the nearest, and on an exact tie away from zero (`(0.5).toFixed(0)` is "1", `(-1.25).toFixed(1)` is "-1.3"; `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is "1.00" because 1.005 is really 1.00499…).

members.name: toExponential
members.doc:
Exponential notation with `digits` (0 to 100) digits after the point, rounded like JS (to
the nearest, an exact tie away from zero): `(123.456).toExponential(2)` is "1.23e+2". Without
`digits`, as many as it takes to tell the value apart (`(123.456).toExponential()` is
"1.23456e+2"). `digits` is truncated as in JS (2.7 is 2, NaN is 0). `NaN` and ±Infinity are
`String(x)`, whatever `digits` is.
members.summary: Exponential notation with `digits` (0 to 100) digits after the point, rounded like JS (to the nearest, an exact tie away from zero): `(123.456).toExponential(2)` is "1.23e+2".

members.name: toPrecision
members.doc:
`precision` (1 to 100) significant digits, rounded like `toExponential`, in fixed notation
unless the exponent is below -6 or at least `precision`: `(123.456).toPrecision(4)` is
"123.5", `(123.456).toPrecision(2)` is "1.2e+2". `precision` is truncated as in JS (2.7 is
2). Without `precision`, `String(x)`.
members.summary: `precision` (1 to 100) significant digits, rounded like `toExponential`, in fixed notation unless the exponent is below -6 or at least `precision`: `(123.456).toPrecision(4)` is "123.5", `(123.456).toPrecision(2)` is "1.2e+2".

`x.toString(radix)` on a float: the compiler compiles a `toString` call with an argument to

fractions are written until they tell `x` apart from its neighbours. `NaN` and ±Infinity are
`String(x)`; a radix outside 2 to 36 is a RangeError.
exports.summary: `x.toString(radix)` on a float: the compiler compiles a `toString` call with an argument to it.

exports.name: promiseNew
exports.signature: function promiseNew<T, E>(executor: (resolve: (value: T) => void, reject: (reason: E) => void) => void throws E): Promise<T, E>
exports.doc:
`new Promise<T, E>((resolve, reject) => ...)`: the compiler compiles the constructor to a call
of `promiseNew`. The executor runs at once and is released before anything waits, so
it can't keep the promise pending through a cycle; `resolve` and `reject` may be stored and
called later, from any task, and the first settlement wins. An error the executor throws
rejects the promise. A promise whose `resolve` and `reject` are all dropped without settling
never settles, like in JS: what awaits it waits until nothing else can happen, and the program
ends then.
exports.summary: `new Promise<T, E>((resolve, reject) => ...)`: the compiler compiles the constructor to a call of `promiseNew`.

that settle it.
exports.summary: What `Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()` returns (ES2024): a pending promise and the functions that settle it.

exports.name: promiseWithResolvers

`Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()`: the compiler compiles it to a call of `promiseWithResolvers`.
`resolve` and `reject` behave like a `new Promise` executor's: they may be stored, sent over
a channel or moved into a spawned task and called there, and the first settlement wins. A
promise whose `resolve` and `reject` are all dropped without settling never settles.
exports.summary: `Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()`: the compiler compiles it to a call of `promiseWithResolvers`.

modules.doc:
Prelude: `Record<K, V>` (docs/internals/design/record.md), a dictionary keyed by strings, a
union of string literal types or a string enum, and the TypeScript `Object` helpers over it.

A record has no members of its own: `r.name` reads the key "name". Sema turns `r[k]`, `r.name`,
`r[k] = v`, `delete r[k]` and object literals typed as a record into calls of the `__`
methods below (`__get` for string keys, `__at` for literal keys, which are always present).
Entries keep JavaScript's order: keys that are array indices (canonical `"0"` to
`"4294967294"`) first, ascending, then the others in insertion order. A key that is an array
index marks the record `unordered`; then the readers (`__keyNames`, `__values`, `__entries`,
and the JSON and formatting glue through `__positions`) sort the entries they read, without
changing the record (they borrow it). A record without such keys pays one byte test per new
key (`Map.__newestKeyDigit`, then `arrayIndex` for a key that starts with a digit). JSON reads
and writes a record as an object (a decoded record is checked for such keys once,
`__decoded`), and `console.log` shows it like one.
modules.summary: Prelude: `Record<K, V>` (docs/internals/design/record.md), a dictionary keyed by strings, a union of string literal types or a string enum, and the TypeScript `Object` helpers over it.

exports.name: Record
exports.doc:
A dictionary from keys of type `K` to values of type `V`, like TypeScript's `Record<K, V>`:
`K` is `string`, a union of string literal types or a string enum. `r.name` and `r[k]` read
a key, `r[k] = v` sets it, `delete r[k]` removes it; entries keep JavaScript's order
(array-index keys first, ascending, then insertion order).
exports.summary: A dictionary from keys of type `K` to values of type `V`, like TypeScript's `Record<K, V>`: `K` is `string`, a union of string literal types or a string enum.

members.name: __at
members.doc: A literal-key record holds every key (sema checks literals; JSON checks documents).
members.summary: A literal-key record holds every key (sema checks literals; JSON checks documents).

members.name: __decoded
members.doc: After JSON decoding (in document order): `unordered` when a key is an array index.
members.summary: After JSON decoding (in document order): `unordered` when a key is an array index.

members.doc:
The order of the live entries (indexes into `keys()` / `values()`) in JavaScript's order:
array indices first, ascending, then the other keys in insertion order (a stable sort).
Empty when the entries are in that order already.

modules.doc:
Prelude: in-place array sorting (`sort`), and `toSorted`, which sorts a copy.

- `sort()` on arrays of numbers and strings: ascending, pattern-defeating quicksort
  (pdqsort, Orson Peters): median-of-3 / ninther pivots, branchless Lomuto partitioning
  (as in Rust's `sort_unstable`), a separate pass for runs of keys equal to the previous
  pivot, detection of already-sorted / reversed input, insertion sort for short ranges and
  heapsort once too many partitions come out unbalanced. O(n log n) worst case, no
  allocation. Not stable, which is unobservable for these types. Floats sort NaN last (a
  total order, so the algorithm's invariants hold).
- `sort(cmp)` for any element type (and on numbers and strings too): **stable** like JS
  `Array.prototype.sort(cmp)`.
  The shape of Rust's driftsort through a scratch buffer of the array's length: natural
  runs, stable quicksort between them, merges (std/sort/stable.vlt). O(n log n), O(n) on
  sorted or reversed input.
  `cmp(a, b)` returns < 0 when `a` goes first, > 0 when `b` goes first, 0 when equivalent
  (on `f64[]` a NaN result counts as 0). Any comparator, even an inconsistent one, gives
  some permutation of the elements.
Elements are never copied or cloned: pdqsort swaps them, the stable sort moves them between
the array and its buffer, so every algorithm here works for any `T`.
There is no generic ordering bound yet, so `sort()` is provided per element type. The
comparator returns a `number` as in JS, except on arrays of a declared integer type, where it
returns an `i64` (`(a, b) => a - b` on `i64[]`, or `a.compareTo(b)`).
modules.summary: Prelude: in-place array sorting (`sort`), and `toSorted`, which sorts a copy.

modules.doc:
Prelude: JS string methods, `String.fromCharCode`, `String.fromCodePoint`, `parseInt`,
`parseFloat`, `Number(s)` (runtime string functions, rt_abi_async.md §12.2).

Positions and lengths count UTF-16 code units, as in JavaScript (`"😀".length` is 2): a
position may fall between the two halves of a surrogate pair, and slicing there keeps the
half as a lone surrogate (docs/reference/types.md "Strings"). Positions are `i64` so negative
arguments keep their JS meaning; "absent" is -1 (`indexOf`, `charCodeAt`) where JS would say
-1 or NaN. Inputs are borrowed; every returned string is owned by the caller (a substring of a
static string may itself be static, which is free to drop).

modules.doc:
Prelude: `Mutex<T>` and `RwLock<T>` for `shared(new Mutex<T>(x))` (docs/reference/async.md),
and `Atomic<T>` (docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md). The compiler turns every
call of an `Atomic` method into the instruction with the ordering its call site names; the
bodies here, `seqcst` whatever the ordering (only ever stronger), run only through a
function value of a method.

The compiler implements `new Mutex<T>(x)` (initializes the lock word) and `m.with((v) => ...)`
(lock, run the callback on the value, unlock) on a `Mutex<T>` or `shared<Mutex<T>>`, and
`new RwLock<T>(x)`, `rw.read(f)` and `rw.write(f)` the same way; these declarations only fix
the layout they use: the runtime's 8-byte lock word, then the value (an `RwLock`'s 19 words,
rt_abi_async.md §9.2). Neither is ever Copy
(copying one would duplicate the lock). Their methods are the only way to reach the value.
modules.summary: Prelude: `Mutex<T>` and `RwLock<T>` for `shared(new Mutex<T>(x))` (docs/reference/async.md), and `Atomic<T>` (docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md).

exports.name: Mutex
exports.doc:
A lock around a value of type `T`, for sharing it between tasks and threads:
`shared(new Mutex<T>(x))`. `m.with((v) => …)` locks, runs the callback on the value, then
unlocks; it is the only way to reach the value.
exports.summary: A lock around a value of type `T`, for sharing it between tasks and threads: `shared(new Mutex<T>(x))`.

exports.name: RwLock
exports.doc:
A lock around a value of type `T` that many readers may hold at once:
`shared(new RwLock<T>(x))`. `rw.read((v) => …)` runs the callback on the value while other
readers may run theirs; the callback cannot change the value. `rw.write((v) => …)` runs it
alone, like `Mutex.with`. A writer that has waited a while holds new readers back, so writers
don't starve. A `read` callback cannot run `with` or `write`, or start a promise or task.
exports.summary: A lock around a value of type `T` that many readers may hold at once: `shared(new RwLock<T>(x))`.

exports.name: Atomic
exports.doc:
A number, `bool` or `shared` value that threads read and change at once, without a lock:
`new Atomic<u64>(0)`
(docs/std/sync.md). It is stored in place, as a plain `T`, in the object or array that holds
it, and it is the one part of a `shared<T>` that changes: `s.hits.add(1)` changes the word in
the `shared` value every thread reads. Each method is one instruction (or a short loop where
the CPU has none). `T` is an integer type, `f64`, `f32` or `bool`; a float's `add`, `sub`,
`max` and `min` are compare-and-swap loops. `T` may also be `shared<U>` or `shared<U> | null`:
`load`, `store` and `exchange` then move references, and `compareExchange` compares identity
and returns whether it swapped (docs/std/sync.md). An `Atomic<string>` is the same, except that
`compareExchange` compares contents.

Every method takes a memory ordering, `"seqcst"` when left out, as JavaScript's `Atomics`:
`"relaxed"` (only this word is atomic), `"acquire"` (later reads see what the thread that
released saw), `"release"`, `"acqrel"` (both) or `"seqcst"` (also one order of all `seqcst`
operations). It must be a string literal. An `Atomic` cannot be copied or shared, only used
where it is: `a.load()` reads it.
exports.summary: A number, `bool` or `shared` value that threads read and change at once, without a lock: `new Atomic<u64>(0)` (docs/std/sync.md).

Makes `v` the value if it is `expected`; returns the previous value, which is `expected`

exports.name: ThreadLocal
exports.doc:
One value per thread, a number or `bool`: `const depth = new ThreadLocal<u32>(0)` at module
level (docs/std/sync.md). Each thread starts with the value given and changes its own with
`set`; `get` reads this thread's. A task moves to another thread only at an `await`, so it reads
its own writes until then. It is for code that keeps per-thread state, such as which reader
slot is this thread's: a value a task needs after an `await` belongs in a variable.

constant.

exports.doc:
The types whose `shared` values are read in place, without a lock or a copy: what holds no
`Mutex`, weak reference, promise, function or interface value, and no class with subclasses
or a `clone()` of its own. The compiler knows which, so no type declares it (an `extends` or
`implements` of it is an error). With a type parameter bounded by it (`V extends Frozen`),
generic code reads a `shared<V>` as a `V`, checked where the generic is instantiated.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the global timer functions of TypeScript and Node, `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`,
`setInterval`, `clearInterval`, `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`, and the `Timer` handle they
return (docs/std/timers.md).
`velt:timers` re-exports them next to `delay` and `Ticker`.

A timer takes a callback returning the promise to run, like JS: `setTimeout(() => save(doc),
100)` or `setTimeout(async () => { ... }, 10)` (a promise can't be passed: promises start
when created). The callback runs on the task that created the timer, as a promise of that
task (never at the same time as its other code), so it shares what it captures with the code
around it, as in Node; it runs once the code that created it and the callbacks that code
queued are done. An error it throws is uncaught: it ends the process at the throw, as in Node,
so catch inside it.
A pending timer keeps the process alive after `main` returns, like a Node `Timeout` (a handle):
a timeout until its callback starts, an interval until it is cleared. `unref()` lets the
process exit without it. Spawned tasks and promises are not handles: what keeps them going is
what they wait for (a callback's promise too, once it started).
Timers are ordinary compiled Velt promises: no code pointer is cached anywhere, so `velt dev`
hot reload needs no special handling.
modules.summary: Prelude: the global timer functions of TypeScript and Node, `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearInterval`, `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`, and the `Timer` handle they return (docs/std/timers.md).

Prelude: compile-time type tests for generic code (docs/reference/functions.md "Type tests").
The compiler decides `typeIs<A, B>()` per instantiation, and lowers an `if` on it so that only
the branch it takes runs; `asType<B>(x)` is allowed only inside such a branch. The bodies
here run only through a function value, which the compiler refuses.

modules.doc:
Prelude: `WeakMap<K, V>`, `WeakSet<T>` and `WeakRef<T>` (docs/std/prelude.md#weakmap-weakset-and-weakref), on velt_rt's
weak-reference core (docs/internals/design/weak-refs.md, rt_abi.md "Weak references").

A key (a `WeakSet` member, a `WeakRef` target) must be an object: a class instance, an object
type or an array (sema checks it). The compiler counts its type and makes it, and every type
reachable from a weak map's key and value types, weak-capable: their release tells a weakly
held object apart and removes it from every map and `WeakRef` as it is freed. A map whose
value refers back to its key (`raw -> proxy(raw)`) frees both once nothing else refers to
either (the ephemeron rule).

A map is created in the runtime on its first `set` (`#id` 0 until then): the intrinsic sees
the key and value types there and passes their glue. Maps and refs are bound to the thread
that made them: sema keeps them out of `spawn`, channels and `shared`.
modules.summary: Prelude: `WeakMap<K, V>`, `WeakSet<T>` and `WeakRef<T>` (docs/std/prelude.md#weakmap-weakset-and-weakref), on velt_rt's weak-reference core (docs/internals/design/weak-refs.md, rt_abi.md "Weak references").

modules.doc:
Prelude: `any` and `unknown`, the dynamic value (issue #924, docs/reference/types.md "any
and unknown"), and `object` and `Function`, the dynamic value restricted to objects and to
functions (issue #926, docs/reference/types.md "object and Function").

Both are interfaces every type implements (the compiler adds the implementation): a value
converted to one is boxed with its type's descriptor, the interface table. They share one
representation; `unknown` must be narrowed before use, `any` converts to a typed value with
a check at run time (a `TypeError` when the value has another type).

The file name sorts last, so the prelude modules before it keep their indexes (and the
symbols of programs that use no `any` stay the same).

modules.doc:
Prelude: the containers of interface adapters (issue #1153; docs/reference/types.md "Generic
interfaces with `unknown` arguments").

A `Handler<Map<unknown, unknown>, E>` converted to `Handler<unknown, unknown>` receives an
`unknown` that may hold a map of any type (`Map<string, number>`), whose elements are stored
unboxed. The adapter passes the method a copy holding the elements boxed (`…In`), and when the
method returns writes the copy back into the map it was made from (`…Out`), so the caller's
map sees every change. Each element written back converts to the map's own element types,
checked as a conversion out of `any` is. The helpers for `Set<unknown>` are in
std/collections/set.vlt, which a program naming `Set` loads.

The file name sorts last, so the prelude modules before it keep their indexes. Its bodies
use dynamic operations without making the program pay for them: sema counts a program as
using `any` members only when it converts such a value (`body/expr/iface_adapt.rs`).
modules.summary: Prelude: the containers of interface adapters (issue #1153; docs/reference/types.md "Generic interfaces with `unknown` arguments").

Prelude: the built-in methods of strings, arrays, numbers and booleans called through `any`
(issue #924, docs/reference/types.md "any and unknown"). A call `x.name(args)` on an `any`
is one call through the descriptor of the value held (`AnyCall`); for a string it runs
`__anyStr_<name>(s, args)`, for an array of `T` `__anyArr_<name><T>(a, args)`, for a number
`__anyNum_<name>(n, args)` and for a boolean `__anyBool_<name>(b, args)` (velt_vir
any_builtin.rs finds them by name). The arguments come as an `any[]` and are converted as
JavaScript converts them (`ToString`, `ToIntegerOrInfinity`); the result goes back as an
`any`. A name without a function here is a `TypeError` naming #924.

The file name sorts after the other prelude modules, so their indexes stay the same.

exports.name: __anyToPrimitive
exports.signature: function __anyToPrimitive(v: any, hint: string, at: string): any
exports.doc:
JavaScript's `ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an `any` holding an object or a function (`hint` is
`"string"`, `"default"` or `"number"`; a primitive is its own, which the callers keep, so
this only borrows `v`): an object's `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)`, else its
`valueOf()` and `toString()` (`toString()` first for `"string"`), the first primitive one
returns kept as it is (a number stays a number). A `Date` takes `"default"` as `"string"`. Sema
writes the dispatch over the program's classes into this body (any_prim.rs); other values go
to `__anyToPrimitivePlain`.
exports.summary: JavaScript's `ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an `any` holding an object or a function (`hint` is `"string"`, `"default"` or `"number"`; a primitive is its own, which the callers keep, so this only borrows `v`): an object's `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)`, else its `valueOf()` and `toString()` (`toString()` first for `"string"`), the first primitive one returns kept as it is (a number stays a number).

exports.name: __anyToPrimitivePlain
exports.signature: function __anyToPrimitivePlain(v: any, hint: string, at: string): any
exports.doc:
`ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an object that is no class instance with a `[Symbol.toPrimitive]`,
`valueOf()` or `toString()`: an array as its `join`, an object literal by its own `valueOf` /
`toString` in the hint's order, another object as `Object.prototype.toString` writes it. A
function's `ToPrimitive` is its source text, which a compiled function doesn't keep: `NaN`
stands for it where only its number counts (`"number"`, and `==`, which `"default"` is for
here, because the text is never a number or a boolean).
exports.summary: `ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an object that is no class instance with a `[Symbol.toPrimitive]`, `valueOf()` or `toString()`: an array as its `join`, an object literal by its own `valueOf` / `toString` in the hint's order, another object as `Object.prototype.toString` writes it.

exports.summary: What a `valueOf()`, `toString()` or `[Symbol.toPrimitive]` returned, which must be a primitive.

exports.doc:

`Date` its time, an object its `valueOf()`).

exports.name: __anyRelational

`a < b` (`op` 0), `a > b` (1), `a <= b` (2) or `a >= b` (3) of dynamic values one of which
holds an object or a function: JavaScript's comparison after `ToPrimitive` with hint

exports.name: Stdout
exports.doc:
Standard output as a synchronous byte sink (for strings, `process.stdout.write(s)` needs no
import). Writes are ordered with `console.log` and buffered the same way; a large array
(64 KiB or more) goes straight to the OS from the caller's buffer, without a copy. Portable: no
`/dev/stdout` needed.
