modules.doc:
std/proxy/array: the array methods called on a proxy of an array (`push`, `pop`, `shift`,
`unshift`, `splice`, `map`, `filter`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `includes`,
`indexOf`, `join`, `slice`, `reverse`, `sort`; issue #823, docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and
Reflect").

`p.push(x)` on a proxy reads `push` through the `get` trap. When the trap forwards to an array
(`Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)`), the method it reads is an `__ArrayMethod`, and the call
runs the method's generic algorithm from the ECMAScript specification with the proxy as `this`
(`Proxy.__arrayCall`, which velt_vir's proxy call slot calls): every read of `length` or of an
element, every write, `in` test and delete goes through the traps, in Node's order.
modules.summary: std/proxy/array: the array methods called on a proxy of an array (`push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `map`, `filter`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `includes`, `indexOf`, `join`, `slice`, `reverse`, `sort`; issue #823, docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect").

exports.name: __ArrayMethod
exports.doc:
An array method read through a proxy (`Reflect.get(array, "push")`), or `constructor`
(`Array`): calling it on a proxy runs the method on the proxy. `typeof` and `console.log`
show it as the function it stands for (velt_vir's `is_array_method`); called any other way,
it is not supported yet. Each read makes a new one (the standard library keeps no module
state), so two reads of a method are not `===`.
exports.summary: An array method read through a proxy (`Reflect.get(array, "push")`), or `constructor` (`Array`): calling it on a proxy runs the method on the proxy.

exports.name: __proxyArrayCall
exports.signature: function __proxyArrayCall(p: Proxy, name: string, args: any[], o: any): any
exports.doc:
`Array.prototype[name].apply(o, args)` for the proxy `p` of an array, `o` its receiver: each
method is the steps of `splice` that its own algorithm takes in the same order.
exports.summary: `Array.prototype[name].apply(o, args)` for the proxy `p` of an array, `o` its receiver: each method is the steps of `splice` that its own algorithm takes in the same order.

modules.doc:
std/proxy/ops: the operations on `any` that a proxy answers with its traps, which sema calls
in a program that has loaded `Proxy` (std/prelude/global/proxy.vlt) instead of the prelude's
(std/prelude/zzz_adapt.vlt): a spread, `Object.hasOwn`, `Object.values` / `entries` and
`delete` of an `any`; the operations whose key is a symbol constant (`p[KEY]`, `KEY in p`,
`delete p[KEY]`, `Object.hasOwn(p, KEY)`); and `new Proxy(target, handler)` with a handler
typed `any` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect").

A symbol constant names a member of a typed value by its key name (U+FFFF and `Symbol(d)`,
velt_sema's `symbols.rs`); sema passes both that name and the symbol itself, so a plain value
is read by the name, as before, and a proxy's trap sees the symbol, as in JavaScript.
modules.summary: std/proxy/ops: the operations on `any` that a proxy answers with its traps, which sema calls in a program that has loaded `Proxy` (std/prelude/global/proxy.vlt) instead of the prelude's (std/prelude/zzz_adapt.vlt): a spread, `Object.hasOwn`, `Object.values` / `entries` and `delete` of an `any`; the operations whose key is a symbol constant (`p[KEY]`, `KEY in p`, `delete p[KEY]`, `Object.hasOwn(p, KEY)`); and `new Proxy(target, handler)` with a handler typed `any` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect").

modules.doc:
std/proxy: JavaScript's `Proxy` and `Reflect` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and
Reflect"), globals loaded when a module names one of them (std/prelude/global/proxy.vlt).

A proxy is a dynamic value: `new Proxy(target, handler)` has the type `any` and holds a
`Proxy` object. Its descriptor slots (velt_vir `lower/any_proxy.rs`) call the `__` methods
below, so `p.k` runs the handler's `get` trap, `p.k = v` its `set` trap and `"k" in p` its
`has` trap, each with the target, the key and the proxy itself as the receiver. A trap the
handler leaves out forwards to the target, as in JavaScript. `Reflect.get` / `set` / `has`
do what the operations do on a plain value, and pass the receiver on to a proxy target.

Its bodies use dynamic operations without making the program pay for them: sema counts a
program as using `any` members only when its own code constructs a `Proxy` or calls `Reflect`.
A program that never names them doesn't load this module, and its operations on `any` don't
test for a proxy (velt:proxy/ops).
modules.summary: std/proxy: JavaScript's `Proxy` and `Reflect` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect"), globals loaded when a module names one of them (std/prelude/global/proxy.vlt).

std/random: fast pseudo-random numbers (like JavaScript's `Math.random()`), for simulations,
sampling, shuffling, jitter and load generation. NOT for secrets, tokens or anything an
attacker must not predict: use std/crypto (`randomBytes`, `randomInt`) for those.

Each thread has its own generator (wyrand), seeded from the OS on first use, so concurrent
tasks never contend and every run gives a different sequence.

modules.doc:
std/redis: a Redis client close to ioredis (rt_abi_async.md §14.12), with strings, expiry,
hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, pipelines, transactions and pub/sub.

`connect(url)` opens one connection that is multiplexed: every command from every task goes
over it, pipelined in order, so a `RedisClient` already works as a pool (like ioredis). Use
`duplicate()` for a second connection when a blocking command (BLPOP, …) must not hold up
the others. A lost connection is reopened automatically: commands already sent on it throw
`RedisError` "ECONNRESET" (they may have run), later ones wait while the client reconnects
with backoff (for up to 10 s, then they throw the connect error, e.g. "ECONNREFUSED").
Subscribers do not reconnect.

`RedisClient` is a Copy handle like std/net's `TcpStream` (async methods take `this` by copy,
so it can be used from many tasks at once), released by `close()`. Commands that take several
keys or values take a `string[]`: `del(["a", "b"])`.

Every failure throws `RedisError` with a `code`: the server's error code for error replies
("WRONGTYPE", "ERR", "NOAUTH", …) or an I/O code ("ECONNREFUSED", "ECONNRESET", "EINVAL").
modules.summary: std/redis: a Redis client close to ioredis (rt_abi_async.md §14.12), with strings, expiry, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, pipelines, transactions and pub/sub.

modules.doc:
std/regex: JavaScript-flavoured regular expressions over the runtime's Rust `regex` engine
(rt_abi_async.md §14). Matching is linear-time (no catastrophic backtracking); in exchange
lookaround and backreferences are not supported (compiling them throws `RegExpError`).

Offsets are UTF-16 code units, like every Velt string position (`slice`, `indexOf`).
`\d \w \b` are ASCII-only as in JS; `i m s` flags work as in JS; `g` makes `replace` replace
every match and `y` (sticky) makes `test`/`exec` match only at the start position. Called
without a start (`exec(s)`), a `g` or `y` regex starts at `lastIndex` and updates it, as in JS;
`exec(s, from)` takes the start explicitly and leaves `lastIndex` alone.

The string methods that take a regex (`s.replace(re, …)`, `match`, `matchAll`, `search`,
`split`, `replaceAll`) are the `extend string` block at the end: the compiler sends such a
call there when the first argument is a `RegExp` (velt_sema's `regex_args`).

A `RegExp` owns a runtime handle (released by `[Symbol.dispose]()`); the compiled program is
immutable and can be used from any task.

modules.doc:
velt:simd/bytes: 128-bit SIMD, 8- and 16-bit lanes. Programs import the types from `velt:simd`.

A vector is a value like a number: sixteen `u8` lanes in a `u8x16`, four `f32` in an
`f32x4`. Every method is one instruction, or a few, on x86-64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and
WebAssembly (`simd128`), the same in debug and release builds; the `velt_simd_*` functions
below have no runtime implementation, the compiler emits them inline (rt_abi.md "SIMD").
Comparisons give a mask (`mask8x16`), which `any()`, `first()`, `bitmask()` and `select`
consume. In std the type names are built in; each `export type` below gives a module that
imports one the built-in type.

Generated by scripts/gen-simd-api.py: change the script, not this file.
modules.summary: velt:simd/bytes: 128-bit SIMD, 8- and 16-bit lanes.

members.name: load
members.signature: static load(from: i8[], at: usize = 0): i8x16
members.doc:
The 16 elements of `from` starting at `at`. Panics with a RangeError unless all 16 are
inside the array.
members.summary: The 16 elements of `from` starting at `at`.

members.name: loadOptimistic
members.signature: static loadOptimistic(from: Atomic<i8>[], at: usize = 0): i8x16
members.doc:
The 16 words of `from` starting at `at`, read while other threads may be changing them:
an optimistic read (velt:sync `VersionLatch`). Each lane a word no thread wrote during the
read is that word; a lane a thread was writing is some value, never undefined behaviour,
so check the latch's version (`isUnchanged`) before trusting any lane. One vector load, as
`load` is, where reading the words one by one takes 16 atomic loads. Panics with a
RangeError unless all 16 are inside the array.
members.summary: The 16 words of `from` starting at `at`, read while other threads may be changing them: an optimistic read (velt:sync `VersionLatch`).

members.doc:

`store` check. As the condition of the loop that calls them (`while (i8x16.fits(xs, i))`),
it leaves them nothing to check.
members.summary: Whether the 16 elements of `xs` starting at `at` are inside the array: what `load` and `store` check.

modules.doc:
velt:simd/clmul: carry-less multiplication of 64-bit lanes as methods of `u64x2` (docs/std/simd.md
"Carry-less multiplication"): x86's PCLMULQDQ and ARM's PMULL, the instruction behind CRC
folding and GHASH. `a.clmulLow(b)` is the 128-bit product of the low lanes as polynomials over
GF(2) (XOR instead of addition, no carries), its low 64 bits in lane 0.

Every method always works: it is the instruction where the CPU has it (`u64x2.hasClmulX86()`,
`u64x2.hasClmulArm()`: the runtime's flags, rt_abi.md "SIMD") and otherwise an exact
emulation, a shift and XOR per bit. The checks are false on WebAssembly, in debug (Cranelift)
builds and with `VELT_SIMD_DISABLE=clmul`. Code that would be slower on the emulation than
without the instruction (a table-driven CRC) checks `u64x2.hasClmul()` first; in a function
gated on the extension (`__intrinsic_target("clmul-x86")`, std only) the methods are the bare
instructions.
modules.summary: velt:simd/clmul: carry-less multiplication of 64-bit lanes as methods of `u64x2` (docs/std/simd.md "Carry-less multiplication"): x86's PCLMULQDQ and ARM's PMULL, the instruction behind CRC folding and GHASH.

modules.doc:
velt:simd/floats: 128-bit SIMD, float lanes. Programs import the types from `velt:simd`.

A vector is a value like a number: sixteen `u8` lanes in a `u8x16`, four `f32` in an
`f32x4`. Every method is one instruction, or a few, on x86-64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and
WebAssembly (`simd128`), the same in debug and release builds; the `velt_simd_*` functions
below have no runtime implementation, the compiler emits them inline (rt_abi.md "SIMD").
Comparisons give a mask (`mask8x16`), which `any()`, `first()`, `bitmask()` and `select`
consume. In std the type names are built in; each `export type` below gives a module that
imports one the built-in type.

modules.doc:
velt:simd/sha: the CPU's SHA-1 and SHA-256 instructions as methods of `u32x4` (#1330,
docs/std/simd.md "SHA instructions"): the ARMv8 ones (ACLE `vsha256hq_u32` & co.) and the x86
ones (Intel's `_mm_sha256rnds2_epu32` & co.), named after the instruction, with the operands
in its order and lane 0 the low 32 bits.

Every method always works: it is the instruction where the CPU has it (`u32x4.hasShaArm()`,
`u32x4.hasShaX86()`: the runtime's flags, rt_abi.md "SIMD") and otherwise an exact emulation,
written below from the ARM Architecture Reference Manual's and the Intel SDM's pseudocode. The
checks are false on another architecture, on WebAssembly and in debug (Cranelift) builds, and
with `VELT_SIMD_DISABLE=sha`, which runs the emulation on a CPU that has the instructions.

The instructions are as fast as the checks around them allow: in a loop of them the flag is
read once, before the loop, and tested in every iteration. In a function gated on the
extension (`__intrinsic_target`, std only, as std/crypto.vlt's) the check is true and the
methods are the bare instructions.

velt:simd: the 128-bit SIMD vector types and their masks (docs/std/simd.md).

  import { u8x16, mask8x16 } from "velt:simd";

Importing any of them loads the whole API: the methods are `extend` blocks, which apply
wherever their module is loaded, and the types convert to each other.

Generated by scripts/gen-simd-api.py: change the script, not this file.

modules.doc:
Building blocks of the stable sort (std/sort/stable.vlt): insertion sort, run reversal and
merging sorted runs through a scratch buffer.

`x` goes before `y` when `neg(cmp(x, y))`. Elements move between an array and a scratch
buffer of the same length with `__intrinsic_array_move` (raw bits: no clone, no drop), so
at any time each element is owned by exactly one of the two arrays and the slot it left
holds a stale copy that is only ever overwritten.
modules.summary: Building blocks of the stable sort (std/sort/stable.vlt): insertion sort, run reversal and merging sorted runs through a scratch buffer.

exports.doc: Insertion sort of xs[lo..hi) whose prefix xs[lo..start) is already sorted. Stable.
exports.summary: Insertion sort of xs[lo..hi) whose prefix xs[lo..start) is already sorted.

exports.name: mergeRuns
exports.signature: function mergeRuns<T, C>(xs: T[], scratch: T[], runs: usize[], cmp: (x: T, y: T) => C, neg: (c: C) => bool)
exports.doc:
Merges the sorted runs of xs whose boundaries are `runs` (run k is xs[runs[k]..runs[k + 1]))
into one, ping-ponging with `scratch` (same length; its slots are stale copies or free).
`runs` is consumed.

modules.doc:
The stable sort behind `sort(cmp)` and `toSorted(cmp)` (std/prelude/sort.vlt): the shape of
Rust's driftsort. One scan finds the long natural runs (ascending, or strictly descending
and then reversed, which keeps the sort stable); the stretches between them are sorted by
a stable quicksort; then neighbouring runs are merged pairwise (std/sort/merge.vlt).
O(n log n) comparisons and moves, O(n) for sorted, reversed or sorted-then-appended input.

The quicksort partitions into a scratch buffer as long as the array: elements less than
the pivot fill it from the front in order, the others from the back, and come back in order
(Rust's stable quicksort). Each element is written to both ends and only one cursor moves,
so the loop has no data-dependent branch, and its comparisons do not wait for each other
(a merge's next comparison depends on the previous one, which a comparator that loads from
memory pays for in full). A pivot equal to the one of the enclosing partition separates
the elements equal to it, which are then done: inputs with many duplicates take O(n log k).
Too many unbalanced partitions switch to merge sort (`mergeSortRange`).

Elements move with `__intrinsic_array_move` (raw bits, no clone, no drop): each one is
owned by exactly one array at any time, the slots it left keep stale copies, and the
buffers' lengths go back to 0 before they are dropped. Every partition and merge moves each
element exactly once whatever the comparator answers, and the depth is bounded, so an
inconsistent comparator (NaN results, random answers) gives some permutation: never a
crash, a lost or duplicated element, or a loop.

A comparator can still reach the array through an alias (`const ys = xs`, or a shared object
holding it), so the sort works on buffers of its own:
- Elements that need no drop (numbers, booleans, plain structs) are copied into them and the
  sorted result is written back over the array at the end, as JavaScript does: the
  comparator sees the array unchanged, and what it stores into it is overwritten. A
  comparator that captures nothing reaches no array (there is no mutable module-level
  state, and such elements hold no references), so then a short array is sorted in place,
  without a buffer (for long ones the copy costs nothing measurable).
- Other elements (strings, arrays, objects) are moved, and the array stays empty until the
  sort is done: a store, `pop` or `truncate` through the alias must not drop or take an
  element whose bits the buffers hold. Reading it is out of bounds; what the comparator
  pushes ends up after the sorted elements. This holds for short arrays too, and whatever
  the comparator captures: its arguments are borrows into the array being sorted, and an
  element can itself hold the array (`[string, Holder]` with the holder owning it), so a
  push through it would reallocate the buffer under them.
modules.summary: The stable sort behind `sort(cmp)` and `toSorted(cmp)` (std/prelude/sort.vlt): the shape of Rust's driftsort.

exports.name: stableSort
exports.signature: function stableSort<T, C>(xs: T[], cmp: (x: T, y: T) => C, neg: (c: C) => bool)
exports.doc:
Stable sort of `xs`: `x` goes before `y` when `neg(cmp(x, y))`; equivalent elements keep
their order. (`cmp` and `neg` are passed separately rather than as one `less` closure so
that both stay known closures that the optimizer specializes and inlines.)
exports.summary: Stable sort of `xs`: `x` goes before `y` when `neg(cmp(x, y))`; equivalent elements keep their order.

modules.doc:
velt:sqlite/btree — cursors over the table and index b-trees of a database file, and the
record of the cell a cursor is on (https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#b_tree_pages).

A cursor keeps its path from the root (one page and cell index per level), so `next` climbs
only as far as it must. A payload that fits its page is read in place; one that spills onto
overflow pages is copied into the cursor's scratch buffer first.

modules.doc:
velt:sqlite/engine — the SQLite engine written in Velt: queries over a database file's bytes,
with the statement API of velt:sqlite (docs/std/sqlite_engine.md). Read-only for now: SELECT
with joins, subqueries, CTEs, aggregates, compound selects; writing is step 4 of
docs/internals/design/sqlite-engine.md.

`prepare` parses and plans once and caches the plan per SQL text, so preparing the same text
again is a map lookup. A plan runs as closures composed at prepare time (no bytecode VM); rows
are read straight from the b-tree pages and decoded only for the columns a query uses.
modules.summary: velt:sqlite/engine — the SQLite engine written in Velt: queries over a database file's bytes, with the statement API of velt:sqlite (docs/std/sqlite_engine.md).

velt:sqlite/exec/agg — aggregate functions (count, sum, total, avg, min, max, group_concat,
string_agg) and the groups of an aggregate query (https://sqlite.org/lang_aggfunc.html).

An aggregate query runs its loops once, stepping the accumulators of each row's group; then
each group gives one output row. Columns read outside aggregates ("bare" columns) take the
values of a row of the group, saved as the group steps: the last row, or, with min() or max(),
the row that holds the extreme value, as SQLite does.

exports.name: aggMisuse
exports.signature: function aggMisuse(c: ExprCompiler, e: Expr, sc: Scope, message: string): never
exports.doc:
An aggregate call `e` where it cannot be, with SQLite's message (`message`). Where name
resolution allows no aggregate (another aggregate's arguments or FILTER, LIMIT, and WHERE or
ON of a query that is no aggregate query; `sc` is where the call is written, as SQLite's name
context, whichever query the aggregate belongs to) it is `misuse of aggregate function f()`;
elsewhere (WHERE of an aggregate query, ORDER BY of one that is not, a subquery's result
column owned by a query that cannot take it) it is the code generator's `misuse of
aggregate: f()`. In a core's own GROUP BY, an aggregate it owns gets SQLite's GROUP BY

modules.doc:
velt:sqlite/exec/fp — SQLite's own conversions between doubles and decimal text, ported from
its util.c and printf.c (3.53): `sqlite3FpDecode` (a double's significant digits, rounded as
printf asks), `sqlite3AtoF` (decimal text to a double), and the `%g`, `%f` and `%e` renderings
with the `!` flag. The powers of ten and `sqlite3Fp10Convert2` are velt:sqlite/real's. REAL
values print and parse exactly as C SQLite's, which does not always agree with the shortest
round-trip form (`1.0/3` is 0.33333333333333331 in C's printf and 0.33333333333333332 in
SQLite).

modules.doc:
velt:sqlite/exec/plan — how each FROM item is read: the planner splits WHERE into AND terms
and, per FROM level (in FROM order), picks a rowid lookup, a rowid range, an index prefix of
equalities with a range on the next column, or a full scan; then the loop of each level.

A term an access path answers exactly (a rowid or index equality) is not checked again; a
range term still is, so the index only narrows the rows. A term is checked at the innermost
level it reads (a LEFT JOIN's ON terms at its own level, before the NULL row decision).

modules.doc:
velt:sqlite/exec/source — the FROM items of a query at run time, and the scopes names are
resolved in.

A `Source` is one FROM item: a table read through its b-tree cursor (and, when the plan picks
one, an index cursor whose entries hold some columns and the rowid), or rows a subquery, a
CTE or VALUES produced (materialized). Expressions read its columns while the loops of the
query stand on a row: values are decoded from the record only when read, and the table row
behind an index entry is found only when a column the index lacks is read.
modules.summary: velt:sqlite/exec/source — the FROM items of a query at run time, and the scopes names are resolved in.

read in Velt: the header, b-tree pages, cells, overflow chains and records.

offset of page `n`'s first byte.

velt:sqlite/real — a REAL's text as SQLite writes it (`CAST(r AS TEXT)`, the sqlite3 shell):
`printf("%!.17g", r)`, with SQLite's own decimal conversion (sqlite3FpDecode in util.c, public
domain) ported to Velt so the digits match byte for byte. The conversion finds 18 significant
digits with a 64x64-bit product against a table of powers of ten, rounds them to 17, and tries
shorter forms that still read back as the same double (so 0.1 is "0.1", not
"0.10000000000000001"). `%!g` keeps a ".0" on integral values and switches to an exponent
below 1e-4 or from 1e17 on.

modules.doc:
velt:sqlite/sql/expr — the expressions of SQLite's grammar (parse.y),
by recursive descent. SELECT and the statements are in velt:sqlite/sql/parser, a subclass
(expressions hold subqueries, so they call its `select()`).

Precedence, lowest first (https://sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#operators):
OR; AND; NOT; = == != <> IS IN LIKE GLOB MATCH REGEXP BETWEEN ISNULL NOTNULL;
< <= > >=; & | << >>; + -; * / %; || -> ->>; COLLATE; unary - + ~.
The binary levels are parsed by precedence climbing (`binaryFrom`), and nesting is bounded
(velt:sqlite/sql/cursor's `enter`), so deeply nested input fails with SQLite's error.

modules.doc:
std/sqlite: embedded SQLite (the driver is crate velt_std_sqlite, built on the native-package
SDK and linked into the runtime; rt_abi_async.md §14.11), with an API
close to better-sqlite3.

Synchronous by design: a typical query takes microseconds, less than handing it to a
blocking thread pool and back would cost, and SQLite serializes writers anyway. Run a long
query in `spawn(...)` to keep it off the current task.

Parameters are a value `P` that std turns into JSON (`JSON.stringify`): an object binds by
name (`:id`, `@id`, `$id` all take the field `id`), an array (or a single number or string)
binds `?` by position. int → INTEGER, float → REAL, string → TEXT, bool → 0/1, null → NULL,
`u8[]` → BLOB. Rows are decoded with `JSON.parse<T[]>`'s decoder (the driver hands them to it
in binary form, not as JSON text): each column fills the field of the same name (rename with
`AS`). INTEGER decodes into integer fields exactly (all of i64) and into `f64` fields; REAL
into `f64`; TEXT into `string`; BLOB into `u8[]`; NULL into `T | null` fields. SQLite has no
booleans: a column declared `BOOLEAN` decodes into `bool`, any other 0/1 value (an
expression) needs an integer field.

`Database` is a Copy handle like std/net's sockets: pass and capture it freely and release it
with `close()`; then every copy throws "SQLITE_MISUSE" (closing again does nothing). A
`Statement` owns its handle and releases it when dropped, so `db.prepare(sql).all()` leaks
nothing. Closing the database while statements exist is safe: they then throw
"SQLITE_MISUSE".

modules.doc:
velt:streams: WHATWG streams (https://streams.spec.whatwg.org) as in Node 22: `ReadableStream`
with its default controller and reader. They are globals (docs/std/streams.md).

A stream's state lives in its controller (`ReadableStreamDefaultController`): the queue of
chunks, the pending reads, and the flags of the spec's algorithms (`started`, `pulling`,
`pullAgain`, `closeRequested`). Nothing points back from the controller to the stream or a
reader, so a stream is freed with its last reference (Velt counts references; a cycle would
never be freed). The source's callbacks run in the spec's order: `start` in the constructor,
`pull` once `start` has settled (a microtask later) and again while the queue is below its
high-water mark or a read is waiting, never two at once; a read takes a queued chunk at once.
modules.summary: velt:streams: WHATWG streams (https://streams.spec.whatwg.org) as in Node 22: `ReadableStream` with its default controller and reader.

closes the stream), and `cancel(reason)` when a consumer cancels it. Each may be `async`, and
an error it throws errors the stream.

velt:string_builder — `StringBuilder` (a global): builds a string in place, one buffer that
grows by doubling, so `n` appends cost O(total length) (#1677). Velt's own; JavaScript builds
with `+=` and `join`, which Velt compiles to the same builder.

The builder is the private string `#buf`, which the runtime's builder functions append to in
place. `toString()` returns it shared, without a copy: the next append copies a shared buffer
before writing, as for any string, so the returned text never changes. `take()` hands the
buffer over and empties the builder, with no copy at all. Every call passes `#buf` first, with no argument after
it that is a call: such an argument would make the compiler read `#buf` into a copy first, to
keep its value, and the append would go to the copy.
modules.summary: velt:string_builder — `StringBuilder` (a global): builds a string in place, one buffer that grows by doubling, so `n` appends cost O(total length) (#1677).

A `symbol` is the address of a record the runtime or the compiler made (rt_abi.md "Symbols"),
compared by identity. A module constant initialized with `Symbol("d")` is a record the
compiler emits (as is one initialized with `Symbol.for("k")`, which `Symbol.for` at run time

interface or a class, `{ [KEY]: v }` in an object literal, `o[KEY]` and `KEY in o`. The

modules.doc:
velt:sync/epoch: epoch-based reclamation (Fraser's scheme, as crossbeam-epoch has it) for the
values an `Atomic` of a `shared` value replaces (docs/internals/design/atomics.md
"Reclamation"). Plain Velt on `Atomic`, `ThreadLocal` and `Mutex`.

A thread reads such values inside a *section* (`pin()` … `unpin()`), which announces the
global epoch it saw in its slot. A replaced value is *retired* with the epoch of its retiring:
kept until every thread that was in a section then has left it. The global epoch moves on
only when every thread in a section has seen the current one, so a value retired at epoch `g`
is unreachable once the epoch is `g + 2` steps on, and is dropped then.
modules.summary: velt:sync/epoch: epoch-based reclamation (Fraser's scheme, as crossbeam-epoch has it) for the values an `Atomic` of a `shared` value replaces (docs/internals/design/atomics.md "Reclamation").

exports.name: pin
exports.doc:
Enters a section: until the matching `unpin()`, no value retired from now on is dropped, and
neither is one retired before that this thread can still reach. Sections nest.
exports.summary: Enters a section: until the matching `unpin()`, no value retired from now on is dropped, and neither is one retired before that this thread can still reach.

exports.doc: Leaves the section the last `pin()` entered.
exports.summary: Leaves the section the last `pin()` entered.

exports.name: retire
exports.doc:
Drops `value` once no thread can still be reading it: every thread in a section now has left
it. Call it for a value just taken out of where other threads find it.
exports.summary: Drops `value` once no thread can still be reading it: every thread in a section now has left it.

exports.name: collect
exports.doc:
Moves the epoch on if every thread in a section has seen the current one, then drops every
value retired 2 epochs or more before, on every thread's list. Returns how many it dropped.
exports.summary: Moves the epoch on if every thread in a section has seen the current one, then drops every value retired 2 epochs or more before, on every thread's list.

velt:sync: building blocks for lock-free code on the prelude's `Atomic<T>`
(docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md): `Backoff`, for a loop that waits for
another thread, and `VersionLatch`, the latch word of optimistic lock coupling, which a
concurrent tree keeps in every node (bbtree's `NodeLatch`). Both are plain Velt on the
public `Atomic` API: any package can write its own.
modules.summary: velt:sync: building blocks for lock-free code on the prelude's `Atomic<T>` (docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md): `Backoff`, for a loop that waits for another thread, and `VersionLatch`, the latch word of optimistic lock coupling, which a concurrent tree keeps in every node (bbtree's `NodeLatch`).

exports.name: Backoff
exports.doc:
Waiting for another thread in a loop, twice as long each round: `snooze()` spins
`2^round` CPU spin hints up to `2^SPIN_ROUNDS`, then yields the thread to the OS each round.
Start a fresh one for each wait: `const b = Backoff.create(); while (!ready()) b.snooze();`.
It waits for another thread, never for a task: whatever it waits for must be taken and let go
between two `await`s (use a `Mutex` or a channel to wait for a task).
exports.summary: Waiting for another thread in a loop, twice as long each round: `snooze()` spins `2^round` CPU spin hints up to `2^SPIN_ROUNDS`, then yields the thread to the OS each round.

exports.name: VersionLatch
exports.doc:
A node's latch word for optimistic lock coupling (bbtree's `NodeLatch`), 8 bytes, kept in
place in a node or an array (`VersionLatch[]`). From the low bit: an exclusive bit, a count of
shared holders, and a version that only grows.

- **Optimistically:** a reader takes `readVersion()`, reads the node while writers may change
  it, then checks `isUnchanged(v)`; if that fails it reads again. A reader writes nothing.
- **Exclusively:** a writer takes the node at the version it read with `tryLockAt(v)` (never
  waiting; start over when it fails), or with `lockExclusive()`, and lets go with
  `unlockExclusive(v)`, which moves it to the next version so readers see it changed.
- **Shared:** `lockShared()` / `unlockShared()` keep writers out without changing the version.

Values read optimistically may be torn until `isUnchanged` says otherwise. Hold the latch only
between `await`s: its waits spin, so a task holding it across an `await` can hang the others.
exports.summary: A node's latch word for optimistic lock coupling (bbtree's `NodeLatch`), 8 bytes, kept in place in a node or an array (`VersionLatch[]`).

exports.name: Atom
exports.doc:
A `shared` value that threads read at once without a lock and replace whole, like Rust's
`arc-swap`: `Atom.create(shared(config))`. Readers never wait and never write; a value it
replaces is dropped once no thread can still be reading it (`velt:sync/epoch`).

- `read((v) => …)` runs the callback on the current value, borrowed: no count, the cheapest
  read. `load()` returns it as a reference of its own, to keep.
- `store(v)` and `swap(v)` replace it (`swap` returns the value before).
- `update((v) => …)` replaces it with what the callback makes of it. Updates take turns, so the
  callback runs once per update, unless a `store` or `swap` came in between (then it runs again
  on the newer value); if it throws, nothing changes. It must not `update` the same `Atom`.

Keep it in a `shared` object for threads to share it, or use an `Atomic<shared<T> | null>`
at module level.
exports.summary: A `shared` value that threads read at once without a lock and replace whole, like Rust's `arc-swap`: `Atom.create(shared(config))`.

modules.doc:
std/task: cancellation, timeouts, task scopes and task placement (docs/std/task.md).

`AbortController` / `AbortSignal` follow TypeScript's shapes. Cancellation is cooperative:
`abort()` sets the signal and wakes the tasks waiting on it; code that accepts a signal checks
it (`throwIfAborted()`) or races its work against `whenAborted()`. Nothing is dropped behind
the program's back, so `finally` blocks and `using` disposal run as usual. There is no
`addEventListener`: the runtime keeps no callbacks (they would break hot reload). Put
`signal.whenAborted()` itself in a `Promise.race` instead: a losing runtime wait is dropped,
whereas an async function wrapped around it would keep waiting.

A signal's runtime object is owned by a `shared` cell (atomic, so `spawn` shares it rather
than copying it) and released once, at the cell's last reference. No handle is public: a
signal is only made by an `AbortController` or the static constructors.
modules.summary: std/task: cancellation, timeouts, task scopes and task placement (docs/std/task.md).

exports.name: timeout
exports.signature: async function timeout<T, E>(p: Promise<T, E>, ms: i64): Promise<T> throws E | TimeoutError
exports.doc:
`p`, unless it does not settle within `ms` milliseconds: then `TimeoutError`. `p` is raced
directly, so after a timeout it is abandoned like a `Promise.race` loser: a runtime wait
(`signal.whenAborted()`, a timer) is dropped, and a started task keeps running, its
rejection handled (pass it a signal to stop it). When `p` wins, the timer is cancelled at
once, so nothing is left waiting.
exports.summary: `p`, unless it does not settle within `ms` milliseconds: then `TimeoutError`.

members.name: signal
members.doc:
The scope's signal: aborted when the body or a child fails (with `cancelOnError`), on
`cancel()`, and when the scope's task is cancelled. Pass it to the children so they stop
cooperatively.
members.summary: The scope's signal: aborted when the body or a child fails (with `cancelOnError`), on `cancel()`, and when the scope's task is cancelled.

members.name: spawn
members.doc:
Adds `p` as a child task of the scope (`spawn(p)`; a call starts on this task, as any
promise value); the scope waits for it. A promise that cannot fail (`Promise<T>`) is
accepted too.
members.summary: Adds `p` as a child task of the scope (`spawn(p)`; a call starts on this task, as any promise value); the scope waits for it.

members.name: cancel
members.doc: Aborts the scope's signal.
members.summary: Aborts the scope's signal.

exports.name: taskScope
exports.signature: async function taskScope<T, E>(body: (scope: TaskScope<E>) => Promise<T> throws E, options: ScopeOptions = {}): Promise<T> throws E
exports.doc:
Structured concurrency: runs `body` with a `TaskScope` and settles only once the body and
every task it spawned with `scope.spawn` have finished, so no child outlives the scope. The
scope fails with the first error in time, of the body or of any child (even one nobody
awaited, or whose error the body caught), and otherwise returns the body's result. With
`cancelOnError` (the default), that first error aborts `scope.signal`, so the other children
can stop; their `AbortError`s come later and don't replace it.
exports.summary: Structured concurrency: runs `body` with a `TaskScope` and settles only once the body and every task it spawned with `scope.spawn` have finished, so no child outlives the scope.

std/test/suite: `describe`, `it`/`test` and the hooks (docs/book/testing.md), as Vitest's.

A call at a test file's top level only queues what it registers (`queued`): it runs when the
program starts, in every process of a test program shared by several files, and must not run
a test file's code there. `velt:test` collects one file's tests (`collect`) in the process
that runs them: it runs the file's queued steps, and with them the `describe` callbacks, whose
calls register into their suite at once.

modules.doc:
std/test: the test runner (docs/book/testing.md). `velt test` finds the test files, compiles
them with a generated `main` that registers their tests here (`__file`, `__test`,
`__testAsync`) and calls `__run`, and starts the program. Everything after that is this module:

- Started by `velt test` (`$VELT_TEST_PLAN` names the plan, a JSON `Plan`), the program is the
  runner: it starts a process per test file, from the program the plan names for the file,
  several at once, and prints their reports in file order, then the summary; its exit code is
  the run's.
- Started for one file (`$VELT_TEST_FILE`, from the test `$VELT_TEST_FROM` on), it runs that
  file's tests one after another and reports each in marker lines for the runner. A failed
  test is an error it throws (a failed `assert` throws an `AssertionError`): it is caught and
  reported, and the next test runs. When a test ends the process (a panic, `process.exit`),
  the runner starts the file again from the test after it. After its last test the process
  exits, whatever timers or servers a failed test left behind.
- Started without either (a test program run by hand or under a debugger), it runs every file's
  tests in this process and prints the report itself.
modules.summary: std/test: the test runner (docs/book/testing.md).

exports.name: Ticker
exports.doc:
A drift-free periodic schedule: tick `k` is due `k * periodMs` after construction (measured
with `performance.now()`), independent of how long the loop body takes. Missed ticks are
skipped, not burst: a `tick()` that is already late resolves at once, and the next one is
the first schedule point after that. A stop wakes a pending tick at once: its sleep races the
stop signal (velt:task), and the losing sleep is cancelled.
exports.summary: A drift-free periodic schedule: tick `k` is due `k * periodMs` after construction (measured with `performance.now()`), independent of how long the loop body takes.

modules.doc:
velt:typed_array/core: `ArrayBuffer`, and `BufferView`, what typed arrays and `DataView` are
(a byte range of a buffer). The small part of the typed arrays that `fetch` bodies need: a
program that uses `Response` loads this module, and the typed array classes only when it
names one or reads `bytes()` (std/prelude/global/fetch_bytes.vlt). Programs use the globals.

An `ArrayBuffer` owns a `u8[]` of fixed length. Views (`Uint8Array`, `Float64Array`,
`DataView`, …) keep a reference to the buffer and a byte range of it, so two views of one
buffer see each other's writes, as in JS.

velt:typed_array/float32_array: `Float32Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an `ArrayBuffer`
(std/typed_array/buffer.vlt) as 32-bit floats (`f32`). Programs use the global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `__index`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

Generated by scripts/gen-typed-arrays.py: change the script, not this file.

velt:typed_array/float64_array: `Float64Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an `ArrayBuffer`
(std/typed_array/buffer.vlt) as 64-bit floats (numbers). Programs use the global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `__index`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

modules.doc:
velt:typed_array/int32_array: `Int32Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an `ArrayBuffer`
(std/typed_array/buffer.vlt) as 32-bit signed integers. Programs use the global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `__index`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

exports.name: Int32Array
exports.signature: class Int32Array extends TypedArray implements Iterable<number>
exports.doc:
An array of 32-bit signed integers in an `ArrayBuffer` (JS `Int32Array`): `new Int32Array(n)` (`n` zeros),
`new Int32Array([1, 2])` (a copy, converted), `new Int32Array(buffer, byteOffset, length)` (a view of
`buffer`, sharing it), or a copy of another typed array.

velt:typed_array: the ES typed arrays and their buffer (docs/std/typed_array.md):
`ArrayBuffer`, `DataView`, `Uint8Array`, `Int8Array`, `Uint8ClampedArray`, `Int16Array`,
`Uint16Array`, `Int32Array`, `Uint32Array`, `Float32Array` and `Float64Array`. Each is also a
global of its own (std/prelude/global/), so a program loads only the classes it names.

exports.name: ArrayBuffer
exports.doc:
A fixed-length block of bytes (JS `ArrayBuffer`). Read and write it through a view:

An array of 32-bit floats (`f32`) in an `ArrayBuffer` (JS `Float32Array`): `new Float32Array(n)` (`n` zeros),

std/url/encode (std-internal): percent-encoding and UTF-8 helpers shared by std/url.

Works on the UTF-8 bytes of a string: an encoder copies them into a `u8[]` once, escapes what
its set asks for, and turns the bytes back into a string once. The copy writes a lone
surrogate as U+FFFD (what `URL` and `URLSearchParams` encode, `%EF%BF%BD`, as WHATWG says);
`encodeURI`/`encodeURIComponent` refuse one instead, and decoding never makes one (surrogate
bytes such as `%ED%A0%BD` are invalid UTF-8). Decoders and `encodeUri` return null where the
public API throws (std/url owns the error class), so this module has no dependency on it.
modules.summary: std/url/encode (std-internal): percent-encoding and UTF-8 helpers shared by std/url.

bracketed IPv6 literals (validated and lowercased but not compressed), and the opaque hosts of
non-special schemes. Not supported: IDNA / punycode — a host that is not ASCII after decoding
is rejected. Every parser returns null where the URL is invalid.

std/url/record (std-internal): the URL record, its parser and serializer, for std/url.

A simplified WHATWG basic URL parser (url.spec.whatwg.org §4.4): the input is split into
scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by scanning for delimiters instead of running the
spec's character state machine, which gives the same results for the inputs the spec accepts
(minus the gaps listed in std/url.vlt). Relative references resolve against a base record
like RFC 3986 §5.2 with WHATWG's special-scheme rules (`\` is a separator, empty hosts are
invalid, default ports are dropped). Parsers return null where the URL is invalid.
modules.summary: std/url/record (std-internal): the URL record, its parser and serializer, for std/url.

modules.doc:
std/url: WHATWG-style `URL` and `URLSearchParams`, plus JS's `encodeURIComponent` family.

Parsing follows the WHATWG URL Standard for the inputs people write (std/url/record.vlt):
special schemes (http https ws wss ftp file) get lowercased hosts, dropped default ports,
`\` as a path separator and dot-segment removal; other schemes keep opaque hosts and paths.
Components are percent-encoded with the spec's encode sets. Known gaps: no IDNA/punycode
(a non-ASCII host is invalid), IPv6 literals are validated loosely and not compressed
(`[0:0::1]` stays as written). `file:` URLs follow the spec's Windows drive-letter rules:
`/x` keeps the base's drive letter, `..` never removes it, a first segment `C|` is `C:`, and a
relative path or a host that starts with a drive letter switches to it.

Mutation: `searchParams` returns a copy; to change the query, edit the copy and assign it
back (`const p = u.searchParams; p.set("a", "1"); u.searchParams = p;`). Setters follow JS:
invalid values are ignored, except `href`, which throws like JS. Like the WHATWG setters, the
ones that run the URL parser drop tabs and newlines from the value first.
modules.summary: std/url: WHATWG-style `URL` and `URLSearchParams`, plus JS's `encodeURIComponent` family.

std/uuid: RFC 9562 UUIDs — random v4, time-ordered v7, parsing, formatting and validation.

Text form is the canonical lowercase `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` (parsing accepts
either case); binary form is 16 bytes in network order. Randomness comes from the OS CSPRNG.
v7 puts the Unix time in milliseconds in the first 48 bits, so v7 ids sort by creation time
(ids created in the same millisecond are ordered randomly: no counter, no module state).

std/websocket/queue (std-internal): the sending side of a connection. Not part of the public
API.

A send encodes its frame into the connection's `SendQueue` at the call, under the queue's
lock, so frames go out in call order from any task, also before a server-side upgrade has
completed. Whoever queues into an idle connection starts its flusher (std/websocket/writer),
which writes everything queued in one write; an idle connection has no task and no buffer.
modules.summary: std/websocket/queue (std-internal): the sending side of a connection.

exports.doc: Queued bytes past which a `send` completes only once the flusher has caught up.
exports.summary: Queued bytes past which a `send` completes only once the flusher has caught up.

exports.summary: Queued, and more than `HIGH_WATER` bytes are waiting.

exports.summary: Not queued: a close frame is queued or was sent.

exports.summary: Not queued: a write failed (`failure` has the error code).

exports.name: DIRECT
exports.doc:
The connection was idle and its reading task has a message in hand with no more input
waiting, so this is most likely its reply in a request/reply exchange: the caller writes the
queue to the socket itself (`writeDirect`), since there is nothing a flusher could batch it
with. (A frame another task sends in that moment is written at once too; only batching is
lost.)

modules.doc:
std/websocket/reader (std-internal): the receiving side of a connection. Not part of the
public API.

The connection's `Reader` holds the bytes read and not yet parsed, and a fragmented message
so far. It lives in the connection's `SendQueue` (std/websocket/queue), under the same lock,
and is only touched in short steps under it: `next` takes a whole message out of
the buffer, or says that more bytes are needed; the task that asked reads them from the
stream with the lock released and hands them over with `feed`. So nothing of the state lives
in a task, one task at a time reads the socket, and the buffer is dropped once every byte in
it is used: an idle connection holds none.
modules.summary: std/websocket/reader (std-internal): the receiving side of a connection.

connection's `Reader` (std/websocket/reader), which `WebSocket.receive` drives itself: the
turn of the task that reads from the stream, and the steps that are neither a message nor a
read (waiting for another task's read, answering a ping or the peer's close frame, failing
the connection on a protocol error). Not part of the public API.

exports.doc: Bytes read at a time.
exports.summary: Bytes read at a time.

exports.name: ReadTurn
exports.doc:
Held by the task that reads from the stream (its step was `READ`): if it is dropped before
it handed over what it read, or its read fails, the next task may read.
exports.summary: Held by the task that reads from the stream (its step was `READ`): if it is dropped before it handed over what it read, or its read fails, the next task may read.

exports.name: other
exports.signature: async function other(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, step: Step): Promise<Step>
exports.doc:
Handles `step`, which is neither a message nor `READ`, and returns the reader's next step
(`CLOSED` after the peer's close frame). Rare, so it is a function of its own: its state is
allocated when it runs instead of being part of every `receive`.
exports.summary: Handles `step`, which is neither a message nor `READ`, and returns the reader's next step (`CLOSED` after the peer's close frame).

modules.doc:
std/websocket/topics (std-internal): publish/subscribe. Not part of the public API.

A publish encodes the frame once and appends the same bytes to every subscriber's queue, so a
message to many sockets costs one encode and one queue append per socket. An idle
subscriber's queue is then written from the publishing task (`writeDirect`): a socket nearly
always takes a frame at once, and a task per subscriber would cost more than the write (on
several threads each one wakes another worker). Only a socket that does not take it all gets
a flusher. A subscriber with more than `PUBLISH_LIMIT` bytes
already queued is skipped for that message, so one slow reader cannot grow the server's
memory without bound (a direct `send` waits instead). Topics are process-wide (one registry,
a runtime slot, rt_abi_async.md §2.2); a connection leaves all of them when it is closed.

Locks, always in this order: the registry, a topic, a connection's queue.
modules.summary: std/websocket/topics (std-internal): publish/subscribe.

exports.name: subscribe
exports.signature: function subscribe(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, topic: string): bool
exports.doc: Subscribes the connection (`stream`, queue `tx`) to `topic`; false if its handle was released.
exports.summary: Subscribes the connection (`stream`, queue `tx`) to `topic`; false if its handle was released.

exports.name: leave
exports.doc: Removes the connection with queue `tx` from `topic`; an emptied topic goes away.
exports.summary: Removes the connection with queue `tx` from `topic`; an emptied topic goes away.

exports.name: unsubscribe
exports.doc: `leave`, also taking `topic` off the connection's own list.
exports.summary: `leave`, also taking `topic` off the connection's own list.

exports.name: publish
exports.signature: function publish(topic: string, frame: u8[], payloadAt: i64, except: Tx | null): i64
exports.doc:
Queues `frame` (a whole unmasked frame whose payload starts at `payloadAt`) for every
subscriber of `topic` except the connection with queue `except` (null: none); the number of
connections.
exports.summary: Queues `frame` (a whole unmasked frame whose payload starts at `payloadAt`) for every subscriber of `topic` except the connection with queue `except` (null: none); the number of connections.

std/websocket/writer (std-internal): the flusher that writes a connection's `SendQueue`, and
what a send or a close waits for. Not part of the public API.
modules.summary: std/websocket/writer (std-internal): the flusher that writes a connection's `SendQueue`, and what a send or a close waits for.

exports.name: CLOSE_FLUSH_MS
exports.doc:
How long a closing connection's flusher gets to write what is queued (a peer that stopped
reading must not keep the socket and its queue alive): 30 s, as the `ws` package.
exports.summary: How long a closing connection's flusher gets to write what is queued (a peer that stopped reading must not keep the socket and its queue alive): 30 s, as the `ws` package.

exports.name: flush
exports.signature: async function flush(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx): Promise<void>
exports.doc:
Writes what is queued, one write per batch, until nothing is: frames queued together (the
replies to messages that arrived together, a broadcast) cost one write. Started by whoever
queued into an idle connection (`START`). On a server-side connection the first write waits
for the upgrade. After the close frame, or a failed write, the socket is shut down and the
queue is stopped.
exports.summary: Writes what is queued, one write per batch, until nothing is: frames queued together (the replies to messages that arrived together, a broadcast) cost one write.

exports.name: flushRest
exports.signature: async function flushRest(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, rest: u8[]): Promise<void>
exports.doc: `flush` after `rest`, what `writeDirect` could not write at once.
exports.summary: `flush` after `rest`, what `writeDirect` could not write at once.

exports.name: writeDirect
exports.doc:
Writes the queue to the socket from the calling task (`DIRECT`: a reply by the connection's
own reading task, with nothing to batch it with). No task is started unless the socket does
not take everything at once, or more was queued meanwhile.
exports.summary: Writes the queue to the socket from the calling task (`DIRECT`: a reply by the connection's own reading task, with nothing to batch it with).

exports.name: start
exports.signature: function start(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, r: i64)
exports.doc: Starts what a queued frame's status `r` asks for: a flusher (`START`) or a direct write.
exports.summary: Starts what a queued frame's status `r` asks for: a flusher (`START`) or a direct write.

exports.name: pongRoom
exports.doc:
Waits until at most `HIGH_WATER` bytes of pongs are queued (never throws): a peer that sends
pings and reads nothing is not read from either until it takes the answers. The application's
own frames do not count, so a ping never stops reading from a peer that is just slow.
exports.summary: Waits until at most `HIGH_WATER` bytes of pongs are queued (never throws): a peer that sends pings and reads nothing is not read from either until it takes the answers.

exports.name: settle
exports.signature: async function settle(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, r: i64): Promise<void>
exports.doc:
Finishes a send whose frame got `r` from the queue: starts the flusher if the connection was
idle, waits for room past the high-water mark, throws if the frame was not queued.
exports.summary: Finishes a send whose frame got `r` from the queue: starts the flusher if the connection was idle, waits for room past the high-water mark, throws if the frame was not queued.

exports.name: settleQuietly
exports.signature: function settleQuietly(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, r: i64)
exports.doc: `settle` for frames the connection sends by itself (pongs, close replies): never throws.
exports.summary: `settle` for frames the connection sends by itself (pongs, close replies): never throws.

exports.name: finish
exports.signature: async function finish(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, flushMs: i64): Promise<void>
exports.doc:
Waits until the flusher has written the close frame (queued by the caller, or earlier) and
stopped; a peer that does not take it within `flushMs` is cut off.
exports.summary: Waits until the flusher has written the close frame (queued by the caller, or earlier) and stopped; a peer that does not take it within `flushMs` is cut off.

exports.name: closeDown
exports.signature: async function closeDown(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, payload: u8[]): Promise<string[] | null>
exports.doc:
The rest of `close()` once the close frame `payload` is known: queues it, waits (bounded) for
the flusher to write it and stop, and releases the queue. Returns the topics the connection
was subscribed to (to leave), or null if the handle was released already.
exports.summary: The rest of `close()` once the close frame `payload` is known: queues it, waits (bounded) for the flusher to write it and stop, and releases the queue.

modules.doc:
std/websocket: WebSocket connections (RFC 6455), accepted by a std/http server or opened as a
client (`ws://`, `wss://`). Written in Velt on std/net streams: framing in
std/websocket/frame, the receiving side in std/websocket/reader and receive, the sending side
in std/websocket/queue and writer, the handshake in std/websocket/handshake, topics in
std/websocket/topics.

Server: inside a `serve` handler, `upgradeWebSocket(req)` claims the connection and gives
back the `101` response the handler must return; talk to the socket from a spawned task:
  if (isWebSocketRequest(req)) {
    const up = upgradeWebSocket(req);
    spawn(session(up.socket));
    return up.response;
  }
Client: `const ws = await connectWebSocket("ws://127.0.0.1:8080/chat");`.

`WebSocket` is a handle like std/net's `TcpStream` (its copies share one connection, so one
task can wait in `receive` while another `send`s), released by `close()`: a `receive` already
waiting then sees the peer's close (null), and later operations through any copy throw
`IoError` `EBADF` ("handle is closed"). Messages are pulled with `receive` (null once the peer
has closed); pings are answered automatically. Only HTTP/1.1 upgrades are supported (HTTP/2
clients fall back to HTTP/1.1 for WebSockets).
modules.summary: std/websocket: WebSocket connections (RFC 6455), accepted by a std/http server or opened as a client (`ws://`, `wss://`).

members.name: close
members.signature: async close(code: i64 = 1000, reason: string = ""): Promise<void>
members.doc:
Sends a close frame (`code` 1000 = normal closure; 1000-1003, 1007-1014 or 3000-4999, else
`IoError` "EINVAL", nothing is sent and the connection stays open) after everything queued,
waits until it is written, and releases the handle. Closing a connection the peer already closed, or closing
twice, is fine; other operations on the handle (through any copy) throw `IoError` `EBADF`
afterwards.
members.summary: Sends a close frame (`code` 1000 = normal closure; 1000-1003, 1007-1014 or 3000-4999, else `IoError` "EINVAL", nothing is sent and the connection stays open) after everything queued, waits until it is written, and releases the handle.

exports.name: publish
exports.signature: function publish(topic: string, text: string): i64
exports.doc:
Sends `text` to every connection subscribed to `topic` (`ws.subscribe`): the frame is encoded
once and queued for each subscriber, which sends it with whatever else is queued. A subscriber
with more than 16 MiB already queued misses the message. Returns the number of connections it
was queued for.
exports.summary: Sends `text` to every connection subscribed to `topic` (`ws.subscribe`): the frame is encoded once and queued for each subscriber, which sends it with whatever else is queued.

exports.doc: Whether `req` asks to be upgraded to a WebSocket.
exports.summary: Whether `req` asks to be upgraded to a WebSocket.

exports.name: upgradeWebSocket
exports.doc:
Accepts a WebSocket upgrade request (throws `IoError` "EINVAL" if `req` is not one, or was
already accepted). Return `response` from the handler; the socket works once that response
has been sent.
exports.summary: Accepts a WebSocket upgrade request (throws `IoError` "EINVAL" if `req` is not one, or was already accepted).

exports.name: acceptWebSocket
exports.signature: function acceptWebSocket(req: HttpRequest, res: HttpResponse): WebSocket | null
exports.doc:
Accepts a WebSocket upgrade request on a `velt:http/server` server: answers `101 Switching
Protocols` with the handshake's accept key and returns the socket (the connection is the
socket's from then on). A request that is not a valid handshake (RFC 6455 §4.2.1: `GET`,
HTTP/1.1, `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`, a key of 16
base64-encoded bytes) is answered here instead (RFC 6455 §4.2.2): 426 with
`Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13` for another version or no upgrade, else 400; it then returns null.
Throws `IoError` "EINVAL" if a response was started.
exports.summary: Accepts a WebSocket upgrade request on a `velt:http/server` server: answers `101 Switching Protocols` with the handshake's accept key and returns the socket (the connection is the socket's from then on).
